lessons.title: Energy Stores, Transfers and Power
lessons.text: Energy Stores Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred between different energy stores . You need to know eight energy stores. Key Fact The eight energy stores are: kinetic, thermal, chemical, elastic potential, gravitational potential, electrostatic, magnetic, and nuclear. Kinetic energy depends on the mass and speed of an object. The equation is: $$E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$$ Where \(E_k\) is kinetic energy in joules (J), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(v\) is speed in metres per second (m/s). Gravitational potential energy depends on the mass, height, and gravitational field strength: $$E_p = m g h$$ Where \(E_p\) is gravitational potential energy in joules, \(m\) is mass in kg, \(g\) is gravitational field strength (10 N/kg on Earth), and \(h\) is height in metres. Elastic Potential Energy Elastic potential energy is stored when an object is stretched or compressed: $$E_e = \frac{1}{2} k e^2$$ Where \(E_e\) is elastic potential energy in J, \(k\) is the spring constant in N/m, and \(e\) is the extension in metres. This only applies up to the limit of proportionality . Energy Transfers Energy moves between stores by four transfer pathways: mechanically (by forces), electrically (by currents), by heating, and by radiation (light, sound, or other waves). When a ball is thrown upwards, energy transfers from the kinetic store to the gravitational potential store. At the top, the ball momentarily stops — all kinetic energy has become gravitational potential energy. As it falls, the transfer reverses. Key Fact The law of conservation of energy states that energy can be transferred usefully, stored, or dissipated — but cannot be created or destroyed. The total energy of a closed system always stays the same. Worked Example: Energy Transfer Calculation A 2 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5 m. Calculate the speed just before it hits the ground (assume no air resistance). Step 1: \(E_p = mgh = 2 \times 10 \times 5 = 100\) J Step 2: Set \(E_k = E_p\), so \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 100\) Step 3: \(v^2 = \frac{2 \times 100}{2} = 100\), so \(v = 10\) m/s Work Done and Power When a force moves an object, work done equals the energy transferred: $$W = F s$$ Where \(W\) is work done in joules, \(F\) is force in newtons (N), and \(s\) is distance along the line of action of the force in metres. Power is the rate of energy transfer: $$P = \frac{E}{t} \quad \text{and} \quad P = \frac{W}{t}$$ Where \(P\) is power in watts (W), \(E\) is energy transferred in joules, and \(t\) is time in seconds. One watt equals one joule per second. Linking Power, Force and Speed If an object moves at constant speed, you can combine the equations: \(P = Fv\), where \(v\) is speed in m/s. This is useful for calculating the power output of engines or motors.

lessons.title: Conservation of Energy, Efficiency and Energy Resources
lessons.text: Conservation of Energy The law of conservation of energy states that energy can never be created or destroyed. In any energy transfer, the total energy before and after is always the same. In a closed system, where nothing can enter or leave, the total energy stays constant. However, in most real-world situations energy is dissipated — it spreads out to the surroundings as thermal energy and becomes increasingly difficult to use. Key Fact Energy is never “lost” — when we say energy is wasted, we mean it has been transferred to less useful stores (usually thermal energy in the surroundings). The total energy in the system has not changed. Efficiency Efficiency tells you how good a device is at transferring energy to useful stores. It is calculated using: $$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output energy}}{\text{total input energy}}$$ Efficiency can also be calculated using power: $$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output power}}{\text{total input power}}$$ Efficiency is a ratio and has no units. It is always between 0 and 1. To express it as a percentage, multiply by 100. No device can ever be more than 100% efficient. Worked Example: Calculating Efficiency A motor uses 500 J of electrical energy and transfers 350 J to the kinetic store. Calculate the efficiency. \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{350}{500} = 0.70\) or 70% This means 70% of the input energy is usefully transferred. The remaining 30% (150 J) is dissipated as thermal energy due to friction and sound. Key Fact Ways to increase efficiency include reducing friction (lubrication, streamlining), using thermal insulation to reduce unwanted heating, and improving design to minimise energy dissipation. Reducing Unwanted Energy Transfers Thermal insulation reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating. In a house, loft insulation, cavity wall insulation, and double glazing all reduce the amount of thermal energy lost to the surroundings. Lubrication reduces friction between moving parts. This means less energy is wasted as heat in the thermal store, so more energy goes to the useful output. Insulation in Buildings The thicker the walls of a house, the slower the rate of thermal energy transfer. Cavity wall insulation traps air between the inner and outer walls. Since air is a poor conductor, this reduces energy transfer by conduction. Double glazing works on the same principle — a layer of gas between two panes of glass reduces conduction and convection. Energy Resources Energy resources can be classified as non-renewable or renewable . Non-renewable resources include fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) and nuclear fuel. These are finite — once used up, they cannot be replaced within a human timescale. Renewable resources include solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, wave power, and biofuels. These are replenished naturally and will not run out. Comparing Energy Resources Fossil fuels are reliable and produce large amounts of energy, but release carbon dioxide (contributing to climate change) and are running out. Nuclear power is reliable and produces no carbon dioxide during operation, but produces radioactive waste that must be stored safely for thousands of years. Renewable resources produce no greenhouse gases during operation and will not run out. However, many are weather-dependent (solar, wind) or location-dependent (tidal, geothermal), and some have high initial costs or low power output compared to fossil fuels. The UK is working towards generating more electricity from renewable sources to reduce carbon emissions and meet climate targets. However, a mix of energy resources is needed to ensure a reliable supply.

lessons.title: Circuits: Current, Resistance and Potential Difference
lessons.text: Electric Current and Charge Electric current is the flow of charge carriers through a conductor. In metals, these charge carriers are electrons that move through the wire when a voltage is applied. Key Fact Current is measured in amperes (A) and represents the amount of charge flowing past a point per second. The equation is \(I = \frac{Q}{t}\) where I is current, Q is charge in coulombs, and t is time in seconds. Current is measured using an ammeter , which must be connected in series with the component you want to measure. This ensures all the current flows through the ammeter. Potential Difference Potential difference (also called voltage) is the driving force that pushes current around a circuit. It represents the energy transferred per coulomb of charge. The equation for potential difference is: $$V = \frac{W}{Q}$$ Where V is potential difference in volts, W is work done (energy transferred) in joules, and Q is charge in coulombs. Measuring Potential Difference Potential difference is measured using a voltmeter . Unlike an ammeter, a voltmeter must be connected in parallel with the component. This allows it to measure the energy difference between the two points without affecting the current flow. Think of potential difference like the height difference in a waterfall — the greater the height difference, the more energy each drop of water has when it reaches the bottom. Resistance and Ohm's Law Resistance opposes the flow of current in a circuit. Different materials and components have different resistances — metals have low resistance while insulators have very high resistance. Key Fact Ohm's Law states that \(V = I \times R\) where V is potential difference in volts, I is current in amperes, and R is resistance in ohms (Ω). This relationship only applies to ohmic conductors at constant temperature. You can rearrange Ohm's law to find any of the three quantities: $$I = \frac{V}{R} \text{ and } R = \frac{V}{I}$$ Factors Affecting Resistance The resistance of a wire depends on four factors: its length (longer = higher resistance), cross-sectional area (thicker = lower resistance), material (different metals have different resistivity), and temperature (higher temperature usually = higher resistance for metals). Some components like filament bulbs are non-ohmic — their resistance changes with temperature, so they don't follow Ohm's law exactly. Series Circuits In a series circuit , components are connected end-to-end in a single loop. Current has only one path to follow. Key Fact In series circuits: current is the same everywhere (\(I_1 = I_2 = I_3\)), potential difference is shared between components (\(V_{total} = V_1 + V_2 + V_3\)), and total resistance equals the sum of individual resistances (\(R_{total} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\)). If one component fails in a series circuit, the whole circuit stops working because the current path is broken. This is why old Christmas lights used to all go out when one bulb failed. Parallel Circuits In a parallel circuit , components are connected on separate branches. Current can follow multiple paths. In parallel circuits, each component receives the full supply voltage. This is why household appliances are connected in parallel — each device gets the full 230V regardless of what other appliances are switched on. Parallel Circuit Rules In parallel circuits: potential difference is the same across each branch (\(V_1 = V_2 = V_3\)), total current equals the sum of branch currents (\(I_{total} = I_1 + I_2 + I_3\)), and total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance. The formula for total resistance in parallel is: \(\frac{1}{R_{total}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3}\) Electrical Power Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer in a circuit. It tells us how quickly electrical energy is being converted to other forms like heat, light or motion. The basic power equation is: $$P = V \times I$$ Where P is power in watts, V is potential difference in volts, and I is current in amperes. By combining this with Ohm's law, we get two more useful equations: \(P = I^2R\) and \(P = \frac{V^2}{R}\).

lessons.title: Series and Parallel Circuits
lessons.text: Series Circuits In a series circuit , all components are connected in a single loop. There is only one path for current to flow, so the current is the same at every point in the circuit. Key Fact In a series circuit: current is the same everywhere, potential differences add up to equal the supply voltage, and total resistance equals the sum of all individual resistances: \(R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\). The potential difference is shared between components in series. The larger the resistance of a component, the greater its share of the total voltage. If two identical resistors are in series, each gets half the supply voltage. Worked Example: Series Circuit A 12 V battery is connected in series with a 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor. Calculate the current and the voltage across each resistor. Step 1: Total resistance \(R_{\text{total}} = 4 + 8 = 12 \; \Omega\) Step 2: Current \(I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{12}{12} = 1\) A (same throughout) Step 3: \(V_1 = IR_1 = 1 \times 4 = 4\) V across the 4 Ω resistor Step 4: \(V_2 = IR_2 = 1 \times 8 = 8\) V across the 8 Ω resistor Check: \(4 + 8 = 12\) V, which equals the supply voltage. Parallel Circuits In a parallel circuit , components are connected on separate branches. Each branch provides a different path for the current to flow through. Key Fact In a parallel circuit: potential difference is the same across each branch, currents in the branches add up to give the total current from the supply, and total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance. The total resistance of resistors in parallel is found using: $$\frac{1}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}$$ Adding more resistors in parallel decreases the total resistance, because there are more paths for the current. This means the total current from the battery increases. Worked Example: Parallel Circuit Two resistors (6 Ω and 3 Ω) are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply. Calculate the current in each branch and the total current. Branch 1: \(I_1 = \frac{V}{R_1} = \frac{12}{6} = 2\) A Branch 2: \(I_2 = \frac{V}{R_2} = \frac{12}{3} = 4\) A Total current: \(I_{\text{total}} = 2 + 4 = 6\) A Investigating Components You need to know the I-V characteristics of three components: fixed resistors (ohmic conductors), filament lamps , and diodes . A fixed resistor gives a straight line through the origin on an I-V graph — current is directly proportional to voltage (Ohm’s law). A filament lamp gives a curve: as current increases, the wire heats up and resistance increases. A diode only conducts in one direction — it has very high resistance in reverse bias. Required Practical: I-V Characteristics To investigate the I-V characteristics of a component, connect it in series with a variable resistor, ammeter, and power supply. Connect a voltmeter in parallel across the component. Vary the resistance using the variable resistor to change the current and voltage. Record pairs of I and V values, then swap the power supply connections to get negative values. Plot V on the x-axis and I on the y-axis. Two other important components are the thermistor and the LDR (light-dependent resistor). A thermistor’s resistance drops as temperature rises, making it useful in temperature sensors. An LDR’s resistance drops as light intensity increases, making it useful in automatic lighting circuits.

lessons.title: Domestic Electricity, Power and the National Grid
lessons.text: Domestic Electricity The UK mains supply is alternating current (a.c.) at about 230 V and a frequency of 50 Hz. This means the current changes direction 50 times per second. Batteries supply direct current (d.c.), which always flows in the same direction. Key Fact UK mains supply: alternating current (a.c.), approximately 230 V, frequency 50 Hz. Batteries supply direct current (d.c.). The Three-Pin Plug Most appliances connect to the mains via a three-pin plug. The three wires are: Live wire (brown) — carries the alternating potential difference from the supply. It alternates between about +325 V and −325 V. Neutral wire (blue) — completes the circuit. It is at, or close to, 0 V (earth potential). Earth wire (green and yellow) — a safety wire connected to the metal casing of an appliance. It carries current to earth if a fault occurs, preventing electric shock. Why the Live Wire Is Dangerous The live wire is dangerous even when the switch is off, because it is still at 230 V relative to earth. If you touch it, a large potential difference exists between you and the ground, causing a current to flow through your body. This can cause serious injury or death. A switch is always connected in the live wire so that when it is off, no current can reach the appliance. Key Fact The fuse is connected in the live wire. If too much current flows (due to a fault), the fuse wire melts, breaking the circuit and preventing overheating or fire. A circuit breaker does the same job but can be reset instead of replaced. Electrical Power and Energy Transfer The power of an appliance tells you how much energy it transfers per second. Two equations link power to current and voltage: $$P = IV$$ $$P = I^2 R$$ Where \(P\) is power in watts, \(I\) is current in amps, \(V\) is potential difference in volts, and \(R\) is resistance in ohms. The energy transferred by an appliance depends on its power and how long it is used: $$E = Pt$$ Where \(E\) is energy in joules, \(P\) is power in watts, and \(t\) is time in seconds. You can also use \(E = QV\), where \(Q\) is charge in coulombs. Worked Example: Energy and Cost A 2 kW kettle is used for 3 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred in joules and in kilowatt-hours. In joules: \(E = Pt = 2000 \times 180 = 360{,}000\) J In kWh: \(E = 2 \times \frac{3}{60} = 0.1\) kWh. If electricity costs 30p per kWh, the cost is \(0.1 \times 30 = 3\)p. The National Grid The National Grid is a network of cables and transformers that distributes electricity from power stations to homes and businesses across the UK. Electricity is transmitted at very high voltages (up to 400,000 V) and low currents. Since power lost as heat in the cables equals \(P = I^2 R\), reducing the current dramatically reduces the energy wasted. Step-Up and Step-Down Transformers Transformers change the voltage of an a.c. supply. A step-up transformer increases the voltage at the power station before transmission. A step-down transformer decreases the voltage near homes to a safe 230 V. When voltage is increased, current decreases (assuming power stays the same: \(P = IV\)). This is why high-voltage transmission wastes less energy — the lower current means less heating in the cables.

lessons.title: Density, States of Matter and Changes of State
lessons.text: What is Density? Density is a measure of how much mass is packed into a given volume. Every material has its own characteristic density, which helps us identify different substances and predict whether they will float or sink. Key Fact Density is calculated using the equation: \(\text{density} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\) or \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\) The unit for density is kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³), though you might also see grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm³). To convert between these units, remember that 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Density Calculation Examples A block of wood has a mass of 800 g and a volume of 1000 cm³. Its density is: $$\rho = \frac{800\text{ g}}{1000\text{ cm}^3} = 0.8\text{ g/cm}^3$$ Since this is less than the density of water (1.0 g/cm³), the wood will float. The Three States of Matter Matter exists in three main states: solid , liquid , and gas . The differences between these states depend on how the particles are arranged and how they move. Key Fact In solids, particles vibrate in fixed positions. In liquids, particles can slide past each other. In gases, particles move freely and rapidly in all directions. Solids In a solid, particles are packed closely together in a regular pattern. They are held in place by strong forces of attraction and can only vibrate about their fixed positions. This gives solids their definite shape and volume. Liquids In a liquid, particles are still close together but not in a regular arrangement. The forces between particles are weaker than in solids, allowing particles to move past each other. This means liquids have a definite volume but take the shape of their container. Gases In a gas, particles are far apart and move randomly at high speeds. The forces between particles are very weak. Gases have no definite shape or volume and will expand to fill any container. Changes of State When we heat or cool a substance, we can change its state. These changes are physical changes — the substance itself doesn’t change, only the arrangement and movement of its particles. The Six Changes of State There are six possible changes of state: Melting: solid → liquid (heating) Freezing: liquid → solid (cooling) Evaporation/Boiling: liquid → gas (heating) Condensation: gas → liquid (cooling) Sublimation: solid → gas (heating) Deposition: gas → solid (cooling) Temperature During Changes of State During a change of state, the temperature remains constant even though we continue to supply energy. This is because the energy is being used to break or form bonds between particles rather than increase their kinetic energy. Key Fact The temperature at which a solid melts is called its melting point. The temperature at which a liquid boils is called its boiling point. These are characteristic properties of each substance. Density Changes During State Changes When a substance changes state, its density usually changes too. This happens because the particles become more or less tightly packed together, changing the volume while the mass stays the same. Generally, solids are denser than liquids, which are denser than gases. However, there are important exceptions — ice is less dense than liquid water, which is why ice floats. Why Ice Floats on Water Water is unusual because its solid form (ice) is less dense than its liquid form. When water freezes, the molecules arrange themselves in a hexagonal crystal structure that takes up more space than the liquid arrangement. Ice has a density of about 0.92 g/cm³ while liquid water has a density of 1.00 g/cm³. This 8% difference is enough to make ice float, which is crucial for life on Earth as it insulates water beneath from freezing completely. Practical Applications Understanding density and states of matter has many practical applications. Engineers use density to choose materials for different purposes — aircraft need low-density materials to reduce weight, while ship anchors need high-density materials to sink effectively. In everyday life, we use changes of state constantly: cooking involves melting butter and boiling water, while refrigeration relies on condensation and evaporation cycles. Exam Tip When calculating density, always check your units carefully. Make sure mass is in kg and volume is in m³ for the standard SI unit of kg/m³. Remember that during changes of state, temperature stays constant — this is a common exam question. Key Takeaways Density equals mass divided by volume and is measured in kg/m³ The three states of matter differ in particle arrangement and movement During changes of state, temperature remains constant while energy breaks or forms particle bonds

lessons.title: Internal Energy, Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat
lessons.text: What is Internal Energy? All matter is made up of particles that are constantly moving. The internal energy of a substance is the total energy stored by all the particles inside it. This energy comes from two sources: The kinetic energy of particles moving around (vibrating, rotating, or moving freely) The potential energy stored in the forces between particles Key Fact Internal energy increases when a substance is heated and decreases when it cools down. The internal energy determines both the temperature and the state of matter. When you heat a substance, you transfer energy to it. This energy makes the particles move faster and can also change how they’re arranged. The amount of internal energy depends on the substance’s temperature, mass, and what material it’s made from. Specific Heat Capacity Different materials need different amounts of energy to heat up by the same amount. For example, water takes much more energy to heat up than copper. This property is called specific heat capacity . Specific Heat Capacity Equation The relationship between energy, mass, temperature change, and specific heat capacity is given by: $$\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta T$$ Where: \(\Delta E\) = change in thermal energy (J) \(m\) = mass (kg) \(c\) = specific heat capacity (J/kg°C) \(\Delta T\) = temperature change (°C) Key Fact Water has a very high specific heat capacity (4200 J/kg°C), which is why it’s good for heating systems and why coastal areas have milder temperatures than inland areas. Materials with high specific heat capacity take more energy to heat up but also store more energy when hot. This makes them good thermal stores . Metals generally have lower specific heat capacities than water, which is why a metal spoon heats up quickly in hot soup. Latent Heat and Changes of State When you heat ice, something interesting happens. At first, the temperature rises as the ice warms up. But when it reaches 0°C, the temperature stops rising even though you’re still adding energy. Instead, the ice melts into water. This energy is called latent heat . Types of Latent Heat There are two main types of latent heat: Latent heat of fusion — energy needed to melt a solid or freeze a liquid Latent heat of vaporisation — energy needed to boil a liquid or condense a gas The latent heat of vaporisation is always much larger than the latent heat of fusion for the same substance. During a change of state, all the energy goes into breaking or forming bonds between particles rather than making them move faster. This is why the temperature stays constant during melting, boiling, condensing, or freezing. The energy required for a change of state is calculated using: \(E = m \times L\), where \(E\) is energy (J), \(m\) is mass (kg), and \(L\) is the specific latent heat (J/kg). Particle Model Explanation The particle model helps explain these energy changes. In a solid, particles vibrate in fixed positions with strong forces holding them together. When heated, particles vibrate more vigorously, increasing the temperature. Energy Changes in Each State Solid to liquid (melting): Energy breaks some bonds between particles. They can now slide past each other but stay close together. Liquid to gas (boiling): Energy completely overcomes forces between particles. They move freely and far apart. Gas to liquid (condensing): Particles lose energy and forces pull them back together. Liquid to solid (freezing): Particles lose more energy and lock into fixed positions. This model explains why gases take up much more space than liquids or solids, and why different substances have different melting and boiling points — it depends on how strong the forces between their particles are.

lessons.title: Atomic Structure, Radioactivity and Half-Life
lessons.text: The Model of the Atom Our understanding of atomic structure has developed over time. The first model was the solid sphere model proposed by Dalton in the early 1800s. He imagined atoms as tiny, indivisible balls. In 1897, J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model — a sphere of positive charge with negative electrons scattered throughout, like plums in a pudding. Key Fact In 1909, Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, but some were deflected and a few bounced back. This proved the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus with electrons orbiting at a distance — the nuclear model . Bohr refined the nuclear model by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances in fixed energy levels (shells). Niels Bohr’s model explained why atoms emit and absorb specific frequencies of electromagnetic radiation. Later, James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932, completing our picture of the atom: a nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in energy levels. Radioactive Decay Some atomic nuclei are radioactive — they are unstable and emit radiation to become more stable. This process is called radioactive decay and is random. You cannot predict when a particular nucleus will decay. Key Fact There are three types of nuclear radiation: alpha (\(\alpha\)) particles, beta (\(\beta\)) particles, and gamma (\(\gamma\)) rays. Each has different properties, penetrating power, and ionising ability. Alpha, Beta and Gamma Radiation Alpha (\(\alpha\)) — two protons and two neutrons (a helium nucleus). Strongly ionising, stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air. The atomic number decreases by 2 and the mass number decreases by 4. Beta (\(\beta\)) — a high-speed electron emitted when a neutron turns into a proton. Moderately ionising, stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. The atomic number increases by 1, mass number stays the same. Gamma (\(\gamma\)) — an electromagnetic wave with no mass or charge. Weakly ionising, only reduced significantly by several centimetres of lead or thick concrete. The atomic number and mass number are unchanged. Half-Life The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time it takes for half the unstable nuclei to decay, or for the count rate (activity) to fall to half its original value. After one half-life, half the original nuclei remain. After two half-lives, a quarter remain. After three half-lives, one-eighth remain, and so on. Worked Example: Half-Life Calculation A sample has an activity of 800 Bq. After 30 minutes, the activity is 100 Bq. Calculate the half-life. 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 = three half-lives Three half-lives = 30 minutes, so one half-life = \(\frac{30}{3} = 10\) minutes. Uses and Hazards of Radiation Nuclear radiation has useful applications: gamma rays are used in medical tracers and to sterilise equipment; beta radiation is used in thickness gauges; alpha sources are used in smoke detectors. Nuclear Contamination and Irradiation Contamination occurs when radioactive material gets onto or inside the body. This is more dangerous because the source stays close to cells. Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an outside source — once the source is removed, the exposure stops. Precautions include: keeping radioactive sources in lead-lined containers, using tongs to handle sources, wearing protective clothing, and minimising exposure time.

lessons.subject: science-aqa
lessons.title: Static Electricity and Electric Fields
lessons.text: Static Charge and Electron Transfer All matter is made of atoms, which contain positively charged protons , negatively charged electrons and neutral neutrons . In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons, so the overall charge is zero. When two insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons are transferred from one surface to the other. The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged, while the material that loses electrons becomes positively charged. This is called static electricity . Key Fact Only electrons move when objects are charged by friction — protons are fixed in the nucleus and cannot transfer between materials. For example, when a polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth, electrons transfer from the cloth to the rod. The rod becomes negatively charged and the cloth becomes positively charged. If a Perspex rod is rubbed with a cloth, electrons transfer from the rod to the cloth, leaving the rod positively charged. Attraction, Repulsion and Sparking Charged objects exert forces on each other without touching. Two objects with the same charge (both positive or both negative) repel each other. Two objects with opposite charges attract each other. A charged object can also attract a neutral object by electrostatic induction — the charge on the nearby object causes electrons in the neutral object to move, creating regions of opposite charge on its surface. Key Fact Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. This rule governs all electrostatic interactions. Sparking and Earthing When a charged object is brought close to an earthed conductor, the potential difference between them can become large enough to ionise the air. Electrons jump across the gap, creating a spark. Lightning is a large-scale example of this — charge builds up in clouds until the potential difference between the cloud and the ground is high enough to cause a massive spark discharge. Earthing allows charge to flow safely to the ground through a conducting path. This prevents dangerous build-up of static charge. Fuel tankers use earthing straps and aircraft are earthed before refuelling to avoid sparks near flammable fuel. Electric Fields A charged object creates an electric field around it. Any other charged object placed in this field will experience a force. The closer to the charged object, the stronger the field — this is shown by field lines drawn closer together. Electric field lines point away from positive charges and towards negative charges. For a single point charge, the field lines are radial (spreading outwards). Between two parallel charged plates, the field is uniform — the field lines are parallel and equally spaced, meaning the force on a charge is the same everywhere between the plates. Field Strength and Force The strength of the electric field depends on the size of the charge producing it and the distance from the charge. A stronger charge creates a stronger field. The field gets weaker as you move further from the charge — this is an example of a non-contact force. The force between two charged objects also depends on both charges and the distance between them. Doubling the distance between charges significantly reduces the force between them. This relationship is important for understanding how charged particles interact in circuits and in everyday static phenomena. Uses and Dangers of Static Electricity Static electricity has practical uses. In electrostatic sprayers, paint or crop spray is given an electric charge so that the droplets repel each other, creating a fine, even mist. The object being sprayed is earthed, so it attracts the charged droplets, reducing waste and giving an even coating — even on the back of the object. In photocopiers and laser printers, static charge is used to attract toner particles to specific areas of a drum, which are then transferred to paper. Electrostatic precipitators in chimneys use charged plates to remove smoke particles from waste gases before they escape into the atmosphere. Dangers of Static Charge Static electricity can be dangerous in certain situations. When refuelling aircraft or filling fuel tankers, friction between flowing fuel and pipes can build up static charge. A spark near flammable fuel vapour could cause an explosion. This is why earthing straps are used and operators touch metal parts before handling fuel nozzles. In hospitals, static sparks near oxygen-rich environments or flammable anaesthetics pose a fire risk. Anti-static flooring and clothing help prevent charge build-up. Similarly, electronic components can be damaged by electrostatic discharge, so technicians wear anti-static wrist straps when handling circuit boards.

lessons.subject: science-aqa
lessons.title: Gas Pressure and Pressure in Fluids
lessons.text: Gas Pressure and the Particle Model Gases consist of particles that are in constant random motion. As these particles collide with the walls of their container, they exert a force on the surface. The total force per unit area is the gas pressure . The more frequent or forceful the collisions, the higher the pressure. Increasing the temperature of a gas gives the particles more kinetic energy, so they move faster and collide with the walls more frequently and with greater force. If the volume of the container is fixed, this increases the pressure. This explains why aerosol cans carry warnings not to heat them — the pressure inside can build up enough to cause an explosion. Key Fact For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the pressure and volume are inversely proportional: \(p \times V = \text{constant}\). This is known as Boyle’s Law. If you compress a gas (reduce its volume), the particles have less space and hit the walls more often, so the pressure increases. If you expand the gas, the particles have more space, collide less often, and the pressure decreases. The relationship is: \(p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2\), where subscripts 1 and 2 refer to the initial and final states. Worked Example: Boyle’s Law Calculation A gas occupies 0.5 m³ at a pressure of 100 kPa. The gas is compressed to 0.2 m³ at constant temperature. What is the new pressure? Using \(p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2\): $$p_2 = \frac{p_1 V_1}{V_2} = \frac{100 \times 0.5}{0.2} = 250 \text{ kPa}$$ Pressure in Fluids and Atmospheric Pressure A fluid is any substance that can flow — both liquids and gases are fluids. Pressure acts in all directions within a fluid. The pressure at any point in a fluid depends on the depth, the density of the fluid and gravitational field strength. The pressure due to a column of liquid is calculated using: $$p = h \rho g$$ where \(p\) is pressure in pascals (Pa), \(h\) is the height of the liquid column in metres, \(\rho\) is the density of the liquid in kg/m³, and \(g\) is gravitational field strength (9.8 N/kg on Earth). Key Fact Pressure in a liquid increases with depth. A diver at 10 m experiences roughly double the atmospheric pressure — one atmosphere from the air above, plus one atmosphere-equivalent from the water. Atmospheric pressure is caused by the weight of air molecules above a surface. At sea level, atmospheric pressure is approximately 101,325 Pa (about 101 kPa). As altitude increases, there are fewer air molecules above, so atmospheric pressure decreases. This is why air pressure is lower on top of a mountain than at sea level. Upthrust and Floating Because pressure increases with depth, the bottom of an object submerged in a fluid experiences a greater pressure than the top. This difference in pressure creates an upward force called upthrust (or buoyancy). If the upthrust equals the weight of the object, it floats. If the weight is greater than the upthrust, the object sinks. An object floats when it displaces a volume of fluid whose weight equals its own weight. This is why a steel ship floats — its hollow shape displaces a large volume of water, creating enough upthrust to support its weight, even though steel is denser than water. Pressure Differences and Everyday Examples Pressure differences cause fluids to flow. When you drink through a straw, you reduce the air pressure inside the straw by expanding your lungs. The higher atmospheric pressure on the surface of the drink pushes the liquid up the straw. Similarly, suction cups work because removing air from inside the cup creates a lower pressure, and atmospheric pressure on the outside holds the cup in place. Hydraulic systems use the fact that pressure is transmitted equally through an incompressible fluid. A small force applied to a small piston creates a pressure that acts equally on a larger piston, producing a larger force. The relationship is: $$\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$$ This principle is used in hydraulic brakes, car jacks and industrial presses. Worked Example: Pressure in a Liquid Calculate the pressure at the bottom of a swimming pool that is 2.5 m deep. The density of water is 1000 kg/m³ and \(g = 9.8\) N/kg. Using \(p = h \rho g\): $$p = 2.5 \times 1000 \times 9.8 = 24{,}500 \text{ Pa} = 24.5 \text{ kPa}$$ This is the pressure from the water alone. The total pressure at the bottom would also include atmospheric pressure (approximately 101 kPa), giving a total of about 125.5 kPa.

lessons.title: Nuclear Radiation: Uses, Fission and Fusion
lessons.text: Nuclear Fission Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller daughter nuclei. This process releases a large amount of energy, along with two or three neutrons and gamma radiation. Fission can occur spontaneously in very unstable isotopes, but in nuclear reactors it is induced by bombarding a fissile nucleus (such as uranium-235 or plutonium-239) with a slow-moving neutron. When a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, it becomes unstable and splits. The two daughter nuclei and the released neutrons carry away kinetic energy. The total mass of the products is slightly less than the mass of the original nucleus plus the neutron — this “missing” mass has been converted into energy according to Einstein’s equation \(E = mc^2\). Key Fact In nuclear fission, the neutrons released can go on to cause further fission events. If at least one neutron from each fission causes another fission, a self-sustaining chain reaction occurs. How a Nuclear Reactor Works In a nuclear power station, the chain reaction must be controlled so that exactly one neutron from each fission event causes another fission. Control rods (made of boron or cadmium) absorb excess neutrons. Lowering the rods into the reactor core slows the reaction; raising them speeds it up. A moderator (usually water or graphite) slows down fast-moving neutrons. Slow neutrons are more likely to be absorbed by uranium-235 nuclei, making fission more likely. The energy from fission heats a coolant (often water), which produces steam to drive turbines connected to generators, producing electricity. Nuclear Fusion Nuclear fusion is the process where two light nuclei join together to form a larger nucleus. This releases a huge amount of energy — even more per kilogram than fission. Fusion is the process that powers stars, including our Sun. In the Sun’s core, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium at temperatures of around 15 million °C. Fusion is difficult to achieve on Earth because the nuclei are positively charged and repel each other. To overcome this electrostatic repulsion, extremely high temperatures and pressures are needed to force the nuclei close enough together for the strong nuclear force to take over and bind them. Maintaining these conditions long enough to sustain a fusion reaction is a major engineering challenge. Key Fact Both fission and fusion release energy because the products have a higher binding energy per nucleon than the reactants. The “missing” mass is converted to energy via \(E = mc^2\). Fusion vs Fission: A Comparison Fission splits large nuclei (like uranium-235) and is used in current nuclear power stations. It produces radioactive waste that must be stored safely for thousands of years. Fusion joins small nuclei (like hydrogen isotopes) and produces far less radioactive waste. However, no commercially viable fusion reactor exists yet because of the extreme conditions required. Both processes convert a small amount of mass into a large amount of energy. Fusion releases more energy per kilogram of fuel and uses hydrogen (abundant in seawater) as fuel, making it a potentially clean and almost unlimited energy source for the future. Uses of Nuclear Radiation Nuclear radiation has many practical applications beyond power generation. In medicine, gamma rays are used in radiotherapy to destroy cancer cells. A focused beam of gamma radiation is aimed at a tumour from multiple angles, concentrating the dose on the cancer while minimising damage to healthy tissue. Radioactive tracers (such as technetium-99m) are injected into the body and tracked using a gamma camera to diagnose conditions like blocked blood vessels or organ function problems. In industry, beta or gamma sources are used to monitor the thickness of materials during manufacturing. If the material gets too thick, less radiation passes through to the detector, triggering an adjustment. Gamma radiation is also used to sterilise medical equipment and food, killing bacteria without chemicals or heat. Choosing the Right Type of Radiation The choice of radiation type depends on its penetrating power and ionising ability. Alpha particles are highly ionising but have very low penetration — they are stopped by a few centimetres of air or a sheet of paper. They are used in smoke detectors, where alpha particles ionise air between two electrodes. When smoke enters, it absorbs the alpha particles, the current drops, and the alarm sounds. Beta particles penetrate further (stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium) and are used for thickness monitoring of thin materials like paper or aluminium foil. Gamma rays are the most penetrating (only significantly reduced by thick lead or concrete) and are chosen for sterilisation and medical imaging because they can pass through the body. Nuclear Waste and Safety Nuclear fission produces radioactive waste, which is categorised as low-level, intermediate-level or high-level depending on its activity and half-life. Low-level waste (contaminated clothing, tools) is compacted and stored in lined, shallow trenches. Intermediate-level waste is mixed with concrete and stored in steel containers. High-level waste (spent fuel rods) generates significant heat and must be cooled before being vitrified (turned into glass) and stored deep underground in geological repositories. Safety precautions when handling radioactive materials include: keeping exposure time as short as possible, maintaining maximum distance from the source, using appropriate shielding (lead-lined containers, thick concrete walls), and monitoring exposure with film badges or electronic dosimeters.

lessons.subject: history-aqa
lessons.title: Elizabeth I: background, character and the royal court
lessons.text: Elizabeth I in 1568 By 1568, Elizabeth Tudor had been Queen of England for ten years. She was 35 years old, unmarried, and ruling alone in a Europe dominated by Catholic kings. The depth study begins here because the next 35 years would test whether a Protestant female monarch could survive the threats of Catholic plots, foreign invasion and political rebellion. Her ability to do so rested on two things: who she was, and the system of patronage she ran from the royal court. Background and Education Elizabeth was the daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn. Her early life was unstable. Her mother was executed when Elizabeth was two; she was declared illegitimate by Parliament; and during the reign of her Catholic half-sister, Mary I (1553–1558), Elizabeth was imprisoned in the Tower for two months under suspicion of plotting. These years taught her caution, secrecy and the value of public popularity — lessons she carried into her reign. Her education, however, was first-class. Tutored by humanist scholars including Roger Ascham, she read Latin, Greek, French and Italian fluently and could translate texts on sight. Contemporaries praised her wit, her command of rhetoric and her ability to argue theology with bishops. She was also musically trained and a skilled horsewoman. This combination of intellect and physical confidence shaped her image as a capable ruler at a time when many doubted any woman could govern. Key Fact Elizabeth’s humanist education (Latin, Greek, theology, rhetoric) and the trauma of imprisonment under Mary I gave her two key tools: the intellectual confidence to argue with ministers and bishops, and the political caution to avoid being trapped by her own decisions. Character: Caution, Image and Anger Elizabeth’s character was a deliberate construction as much as a personality. She delayed major decisions, sometimes for years, because she knew that once a marriage or war was committed, it could not be reversed. Foreign ambassadors complained that she refused to give a straight answer. She also performed authority in public — processions, speeches, jewelled portraits — while keeping her private feelings hidden. Behind closed doors, she could be furious: she slapped courtiers, threw her shoe at Walsingham, and once shouted that Parliament was ‘a meddling pack of wolves’. Yet in public she was ‘Gloriana’, the Virgin Queen, married to her kingdom. Why ‘Gloriana’ mattered Elizabeth could not rely on a husband or a strong army to enforce her authority. Instead she used image-making. The Rainbow Portrait shows her with eyes and ears stitched into her robe, suggesting an all-seeing ruler. The Armada Portrait, painted after 1588, places her hand on a globe to imply English mastery of the seas. These were not just decoration — they were political tools shown to ambassadors and copied for nobles to display in their houses. The Royal Court The royal court was the centre of political power. It was not one fixed building but moved between palaces — Whitehall, Greenwich, Hampton Court, Richmond — and on summer ‘progresses’ through the houses of leading nobles. Around 1,500 people travelled with the queen. The court was where appointments were made, petitions were heard, ambassadors were received, and laws were debated before being passed to Parliament. Access to the queen was tightly controlled. The Privy Chamber was her inner ring. Only senior ministers and trusted favourites — men like Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, and later Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex — could enter freely. For everyone else, a moment in the Presence Chamber, or a place in a procession, was the prize that bound them to the Crown. Patronage: The Glue That Held the Reign Together Patronage was how Elizabeth governed without a standing army or a police force. She had limited cash, but she controlled appointments, monopolies, lands and titles. By granting these to loyal nobles and gentry, she bound them to her interests. A monopoly on sweet wines, for example, was a licence to charge a fee on every cask imported — worth a fortune. Lord-Lieutenancies of counties carried prestige and authority over local militia. Even the right to wear certain fabrics, regulated by sumptuary laws, was a form of patronage. The system worked while the queen kept rivals in balance. Cecil and Leicester pulled in different directions; later, Robert Cecil and Essex did the same. So long as Elizabeth held the rewards, ambitious men competed for her favour rather than uniting against her. The breakdown of this balance, when Essex lost his sweet wine monopoly in 1600, would lead to his rebellion in 1601 — a story for a later lesson. What patronage looked like in practice A typical patronage chain ran like this: a county gentleman wanted a Justice-of-the-Peace post for his son. He approached a courtier with influence — perhaps Burghley’s clerk — and offered loyalty, votes in Parliament, or a gift. The courtier raised the request with Burghley, who raised it with the queen. If granted, the family owed Elizabeth a debt of service that lasted a generation. Multiply this by every county and the queen had a network of obligation across the kingdom. Key Fact Patronage tied nobles and gentry to the Crown by reward, not force. Because Elizabeth controlled who got the lands, monopolies and offices, ambitious men had to compete for her favour rather than challenge her authority — provided she kept the rewards flowing.

triage.why_not: This lesson is primarily biographical narrative and structural explanation. It teaches WHAT Elizabeth was like (caution, image-conscious, intelligent) and HOW the court and patronage system worked—both best conveyed through clear prose. The concepts are abstract relationships (character traits → political survival, patronage chains → loyalty networks) rather than processes or decisions students manipulate. An interactive would distract from the core task: understanding Elizabeth's calculated self-presentation and how she used institutional structures to govern without traditional force. A well-written paragraph explaining the patronage chain teaches this more directly than dragging courtiers around a court diagram would. Save interactives for later lessons where students need to *experience* consequences (Essex's rebellion, marriage negotiations) or *sequence* complex timelines.

lessons.subject: history-aqa
lessons.title: Key ministers: Cecil, Walsingham and the Privy Council
lessons.text: Why Ministers Mattered Elizabeth set policy, but she could not run a kingdom of four million people on her own. Her power depended on a small group of ministers who managed finance, foreign policy, the law, intelligence and the day-to-day flow of royal correspondence. Three names dominate this story: William Cecil (Lord Burghley), Sir Francis Walsingham, and Cecil’s son Robert. Together with the wider Privy Council , they were the engine room of the regime. William Cecil (Lord Burghley) William Cecil served Elizabeth from 1558, the day she became queen, until his death in 1598 — almost the entire reign. He was first her Principal Secretary , then from 1572 Lord Treasurer (chief finance minister), and was made Lord Burghley in 1571. Cecil’s strengths were administration and patience. He kept meticulous notes, drafted memoranda weighing up the pros and cons of every option, and waited for Elizabeth’s decision rather than forcing her hand. The historian John Guy has called him ‘the indispensable man’ of the regime. Cecil was a moderate Protestant who believed England’s safety required peace abroad and stability at home. He pushed for the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, but only after years of building a legal and political case. He resisted ruinously expensive wars but agreed when threats — such as the Spanish Armada — could no longer be avoided. He trained his younger son Robert to take over from him, and on Burghley’s death in 1598 the transition was almost seamless. Key Fact William Cecil (Lord Burghley) was Principal Secretary 1558–1572 and Lord Treasurer 1572–1598 — almost the entire reign. He was the administrator who turned Elizabeth’s decisions into working policy and prepared his son Robert to succeed him. Sir Francis Walsingham, Spymaster If Burghley was the manager, Walsingham was the watchman. Appointed Principal Secretary in 1573, he ran what we would now call an intelligence service. Walsingham was a hard Protestant who believed Catholic Europe — especially Spain — was an existential threat to Elizabethan England. He recruited informants in English Catholic communities, intercepted letters between exiles abroad and plotters at home, and ran double agents inside hostile courts. His most famous coup was the unmasking of the Babington Plot in 1586. Walsingham’s agents intercepted ciphered letters between the conspirators and Mary, Queen of Scots, decrypted them, and even forged a postscript to draw out further names. The evidence convicted Mary, leading to her execution at Fotheringhay Castle in February 1587. Walsingham died in 1590, exhausted and in debt; the queen had paid him too little for the work he had done. How Walsingham’s network worked Walsingham paid agents from his own pocket, partly because the Crown was reluctant to fund spies and partly to keep their identities secret from political rivals. His agents posed as Catholic exiles in Paris and Rome, infiltrated seminaries that were training English priests for missions home, and watched the ports for forbidden books. He developed methods for opening, copying and resealing letters without breaking the wax. Code-breakers including Thomas Phelippes worked in his service. None of this had a formal department; it ran through Walsingham’s personal household. Robert Cecil Robert Cecil, Burghley’s younger son, succeeded his father as the queen’s leading minister. Trained from boyhood for the role, he was small, hunchbacked and famously sharp-tongued. Elizabeth nicknamed him her ‘little elf’. From the mid-1590s he managed both domestic administration and the secret negotiations that, after Elizabeth’s death in 1603, would secure the peaceful succession of James VI of Scotland as James I of England. His clash with Essex, who saw the Cecils as rivals blocking his ambition, would set up the rebellion of 1601. The Privy Council The Privy Council was the queen’s inner advisory body. Around 19–20 men, all hand-picked, met two or three times a week. They debated foreign policy, military matters, religious enforcement, the granting of monopolies, the management of the harvest and law-and-order issues that came to the Crown. Notes were kept by the Clerk of the Council; decisions were sent out as letters carrying Elizabeth’s authority. Elizabeth used the Council as a sounding board. She did not always attend meetings; instead, ministers debated, summarised the options for her, and waited for her ruling. She often picked apart their conclusions and demanded more information. This style frustrated councillors but kept ultimate authority firmly in her hands. As historian Penry Williams put it, the Council advised; the queen decided. Common misconception: Mary, Queen of Scots vs Mary I The Mary mentioned in this lesson is Mary, Queen of Scots — Elizabeth’s Catholic Stuart cousin, executed in 1587. She is not Mary I (also called Mary Tudor or ‘Bloody Mary’), who was Elizabeth’s half-sister and queen of England 1553–1558. Mary I died ten years before this depth study begins. Mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes in Elizabethan exam answers. Key Fact Cecil ran administration and finance; Walsingham ran intelligence and uncovered the Babington Plot of 1586; the Privy Council debated policy and turned the queen’s decisions into instructions sent to officials across the kingdom.

lessons.subject: history-aqa
lessons.title: A female ruler: Parliament, marriage and the succession
lessons.text: A Woman on the Throne A queen ruling alone was unusual in sixteenth-century Europe. Most political theorists, churchmen and Members of Parliament assumed that a woman should be guided by her father, husband or king. The Scottish reformer John Knox had even written a pamphlet in 1558 attacking the ‘monstrous regiment of women’. Elizabeth therefore inherited a problem that her father, Henry VIII, had never faced: many of her own subjects believed her sex unfitted her for the role. How she handled Parliament, the question of marriage, and the succession defined her authority for the next 35 years. Parliament: Useful but Pushy Elizabeth needed Parliament. Only Parliament could grant taxation (subsidies) to fund the Crown, and only an Act of Parliament had the legal weight to settle religion or change the law of succession. Yet Parliament also held views Elizabeth disliked. Many MPs were strongly Protestant and wanted further religious reform; many were anxious about the unmarried queen and pressed her to choose a husband or name an heir. Elizabeth’s answer was to call Parliament rarely — only ten times in 45 years — and to limit what it discussed. Two clashes show the pattern. In 1566, MPs led by Paul Wentworth demanded that Elizabeth either marry or name a successor. She replied that the matter was a matter of prerogative — her decision alone — and forbade discussion. In 1576, Peter Wentworth (Paul’s brother) argued that Parliament had a right to free speech on any subject; he was sent to the Tower. Elizabeth let Parliament grant her money, but on her terms. Key Fact Elizabeth called Parliament only ten times between 1559 and 1601. She accepted its right to grant taxation and pass laws but ruled that the queen’s marriage and the succession were matters of royal prerogative and not for MPs to debate. The Marriage Question From the day she became queen, ministers and ambassadors expected Elizabeth to marry. A husband would, they assumed, give her political guidance, military support and an heir. Suitors lined up for almost two decades. Philip II of Spain (her dead sister’s husband) proposed within months. Archduke Charles of Austria was considered seriously through the 1560s. King Erik XIV of Sweden sent expensive gifts. Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, was her favourite at home but was suspected of murdering his wife and could never be openly courted. Last in line was Francis, Duke of Anjou, the French king’s brother, who came close to a deal in 1581. Elizabeth said she preferred to remain the Virgin Queen . Each potential match brought drawbacks: a Catholic husband risked the religious settlement; a foreign prince risked drawing England into European wars; a domestic noble risked civil war between rival factions. Delay was, for Elizabeth, almost always safer than commitment. By the late 1570s she was past the typical age for childbirth, and by 1581 the marriage question was effectively closed. Why Elizabeth treated marriage as a tool, not a goal Elizabeth used marriage negotiations as diplomacy. While Spain and France believed she might still wed their candidate, neither dared invade. Negotiations with the Duke of Anjou in 1581, for example, helped delay open war with Spain by several years. The image of an ‘available’ queen was politically useful even when the reality was that no marriage would happen. The historian Wallace MacCaffrey called this her ‘permanent ambiguity’. The Succession Problem No marriage meant no obvious heir. The senior Catholic claimant was Mary, Queen of Scots, the queen’s cousin. After Mary’s execution in 1587, the heir most ministers favoured was her Protestant son James VI of Scotland. Elizabeth refused to name him publicly. Naming an heir, she argued, would attract plotters — people would ‘set their eyes on the rising sun’. Yet the silence created the opposite anxiety: that her death might trigger civil war. The risk grew through the 1590s. In 1595 the Catholic exile Robert Persons published a book arguing for the Spanish royal family’s right to the English throne. Robert Cecil therefore opened a secret correspondence with James VI, encouraging him to be patient and assuring him of support. When Elizabeth died on 24 March 1603, James was proclaimed king within hours. The succession was settled peacefully — but only because Cecil had quietly prepared the ground while the queen herself stayed silent. Two Marys to keep separate The succession debate involves Mary, Queen of Scots — Elizabeth’s Catholic Stuart cousin who was held in England from 1568 and executed in 1587. She is not Mary I (Elizabeth’s Tudor half-sister), who died in 1558 before this depth study begins. Examiners flag this confusion every year as a top reason exam answers lose marks. Key Fact Elizabeth refused to name an heir to avoid creating a focus for plots. After Mary, Queen of Scots, was executed in 1587, Robert Cecil secretly prepared the way for Mary’s Protestant son, James VI of Scotland, who was proclaimed King James I within hours of Elizabeth’s death in March 1603.

lessons.subject: history-aqa
lessons.title: Authority at the end of the reign and Essex's rebellion (1601)
lessons.text: Authority Under Strain in the 1590s By the 1590s Elizabeth was an old queen. She was 60 in 1593 and her ministers, courtiers and people knew she could not rule for much longer. The decade brought a run of crises: a long, expensive war with Spain after 1588; rebellion in Ireland led by the Earl of Tyrone; four bad harvests between 1594 and 1598 that pushed the price of grain above the reach of labourers; outbreaks of plague; and the deaths of Walsingham (1590) and Burghley (1598). Yet Elizabeth’s authority held, even as one of her own favourites — Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex — rose, fell and led a rebellion . Why Authority Held Elizabeth’s grip on power into the 1590s rested on five things. First, the patronage system — lands, monopolies, county offices — still flowed from her, so ambitious men competed for her favour. Second, the cult of Gloriana projected an unaging queen onto portraits and progresses, even as her health declined. Third, the long shadow of the 1588 Armada victory gave her credit she could draw on for years. Fourth, Robert Cecil quietly took on his father’s administrative weight after 1598. Fifth, the queen herself remained the source of final decisions; ministers competed for influence, but she chose between them. Key Fact Despite the war with Spain, Tyrone’s rebellion in Ireland, four bad harvests (1594–1598) and the deaths of Walsingham (1590) and Burghley (1598), Elizabeth kept her authority through patronage, the Gloriana image, the legacy of 1588, and Robert Cecil’s steady administration. The Rise of Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex, was the stepson of Robert Dudley and Elizabeth’s closest court favourite from the late 1580s. He was charming, brave, well-educated and 33 years younger than the queen. He led English troops in France in 1591 and helped capture Cadiz from the Spanish in 1596. He cultivated a public image as a chivalrous war-leader at a time when the Cecil faction at court favoured negotiation. By the late 1590s he expected to inherit the senior offices that Burghley had held. But Essex was rash. He quarrelled openly with the queen; on one famous occasion in 1598 he half-drew his sword at her in the Privy Chamber, an offence that another courtier would have died for. He treated the rivalry with Robert Cecil as a personal feud. He surrounded himself with discontented young nobles and military veterans — a pattern Walsingham’s old intelligence service watched closely. Ireland and the Loss of Patronage In 1599 Elizabeth sent Essex to Ireland with a large army to crush the rebellion of Hugh O’Neill, Earl of Tyrone. The campaign was a disaster. Essex avoided battle, made a private truce with Tyrone, and then abandoned his command and sailed home without permission. He burst, mud-stained, into the queen’s bedchamber at Nonsuch Palace in September 1599 — an unforgivable breach of royal protocol. He was placed under house arrest and forbidden the court. The decisive blow came in 1600. Elizabeth refused to renew Essex’s monopoly on sweet wines, the income source on which his lavish household and political following depended. Without that patronage, his creditors closed in and his political support began to drain away. As we saw in earlier lessons, patronage was the glue that held the Elizabethan elite to the Crown. When Elizabeth withdrew it from a great noble whose followers had been promised offices and rewards, those followers had nowhere to go — except into rebellion. Why losing the sweet wines monopoly mattered A monopoly on sweet wines meant that Essex could charge a fee on every cask of imported sweet wine sold in England. The income paid for his household, his agents, his soldiers and his political dependents. When Elizabeth let the licence lapse in October 1600, his finances collapsed within months. Several historians, including Penry Williams, see this single decision as the trigger for the rebellion: Essex was not yet ruined, but he believed he soon would be. Essex’s Rebellion, February 1601 On 8 February 1601, Essex marched out of his London home, Essex House on the Strand, with about 200–300 followers, mostly armed. His plan was to seize the queen, force her to dismiss Robert Cecil and pardon him. He hoped Londoners would join him as he walked through the city. They did not. The Privy Council acted fast: Cecil had been warned by informants and had already declared Essex a traitor. Royal heralds rode through the streets repeating the proclamation. By that afternoon Essex’s followers were melting away. He surrendered at Essex House by evening. A trial followed at Westminster on 19 February. Essex was found guilty of treason. He was beheaded at the Tower on 25 February 1601, the last execution of an Elizabethan favourite. About five other ringleaders were also executed; the rest of the followers were fined or pardoned. Cecil, Essex’s rival, emerged unchallenged as the queen’s leading minister. The Richard II performance On 7 February 1601, the day before the rising, Essex’s supporters paid Shakespeare’s company, the Lord Chamberlain’s Men, to stage Richard II — a play that depicts the deposition of an unpopular monarch. They hoped it would prepare London opinion. The performance went ahead but failed in its political purpose; the company itself was investigated but cleared, on the grounds that they had simply taken paying customers. Elizabeth later remarked, ‘I am Richard II, know ye not that?’. Key Fact Essex’s rebellion failed within hours because Robert Cecil had been warned in advance, declared him a traitor, and got royal heralds onto the streets faster than Essex could rally support. Patronage withdrawn from one ambitious man could not be replaced overnight by armed force.

lessons.subject: history-aqa
lessons.title: Religious matters: settlement, Catholics and Puritans
lessons.text: The Religious Inheritance of 1568 When this depth study opens in 1568, England’s religion had changed three times in a single generation. Henry VIII broke with Rome in the 1530s; Edward VI made the country firmly Protestant; Mary I restored Catholicism and burned around 280 Protestants. When Elizabeth came to the throne in 1558 she had to settle the question for a fourth time. The compromise she chose — the Religious Settlement of 1559 — would shape the next 35 years. The Religious Settlement, 1559 The settlement was carried by two laws. The Act of Supremacy made Elizabeth ‘Supreme Governor’ of the Church of England (not ‘Supreme Head’, a title some thought wrong for a woman) and required clergy and officials to swear an oath of loyalty. The Act of Uniformity imposed a new English Book of Common Prayer on every parish, set out the form of services, and required attendance at Sunday worship. Those who failed to attend faced a fine of 12 pence. The Settlement was deliberately a middle way. Doctrine was Protestant: the 39 Articles of 1563 affirmed salvation by faith and rejected the Catholic mass as a sacrifice. But the appearance of services kept some traditional Catholic features: priests wore vestments, churches kept altars, and the Prayer Book’s wording on communion was carefully ambiguous so that both Protestants and many Catholics could attend. Elizabeth’s aim was outward conformity — she famously said she had ‘no desire to make windows into men’s souls’. Key Fact The 1559 Religious Settlement was carried by two Acts: the Act of Supremacy (Elizabeth as Supreme Governor of the Church of England) and the Act of Uniformity (one English Prayer Book, compulsory Sunday attendance, 12-pence fine for staying away). English Catholics In 1568 a large minority of the population was still Catholic, especially in the north and west. Most attended Anglican services to avoid the fine and were nicknamed ‘ Church Papists ’. A smaller, more determined group refused to attend at all. They were called recusants — from the Latin ‘recusare’, ‘to refuse’. Elizabeth and her ministers initially treated Catholics cautiously. The fines were enforced loosely; few priests were arrested in the 1560s; and the queen even tolerated private Catholic worship in some great households. Her concern was political loyalty, not theological purity. This relatively soft approach would harden sharply after 1569 (the Northern Rebellion) and 1570 (her excommunication) — the subject of the next lesson. The Puritans If Catholics found the Settlement too Protestant, the Puritans found it not Protestant enough. ‘Puritan’ was originally a term of insult for hardline Protestants who wanted to ‘purify’ the Church of remaining Catholic features. Their objections were specific: vestments looked too Catholic; the Prayer Book’s communion wording was too vague; bishops’ authority was too like the Roman hierarchy; church courts and saints’ days were superstition. Puritans wanted simpler services, more preaching, and church government by elected elders rather than bishops appointed by the Crown. Puritans were not a single party. Many remained inside the Church of England and worked for reform from within — pressing through Parliament for changes to the Prayer Book. Others were Presbyterians, who wanted bishops abolished entirely. A small minority were Separatists, who left the Church to form independent congregations. Elizabeth saw the most radical Puritans as a political threat — their attacks on bishops, she argued, were attacks on her own authority over the Church. The Vestments Controversy and the Prophesyings In the 1560s some Puritan clergy refused to wear the surplice, the white robe required by the Prayer Book. Archbishop Parker, on Elizabeth’s orders, suspended around 37 London ministers in 1566. In the 1570s Puritans organised ‘prophesyings’ — meetings to discuss Bible passages and improve preaching. Archbishop Grindal refused to suppress them, arguing that better preaching was good for the Church. Elizabeth disagreed and suspended Grindal in 1577. After his death in 1583, John Whitgift was made archbishop with orders to enforce conformity strictly. The Government’s Response, 1568–1603 Through the reign, the regime tightened the rules whenever a threat appeared. Recusancy fines rose sharply in 1581 (from 12 pence per Sunday to £20 per month). The 1585 Act made it treason to be a Catholic priest trained abroad and entering England; up to 130 priests were executed by 1603. From the 1580s, Whitgift’s ‘Three Articles’ required every clergyman to accept the queen’s supremacy, the Prayer Book and the 39 Articles. Roughly 200 Puritan ministers were deprived of their parishes for refusing. How ‘outward conformity’ actually worked For most ordinary parishioners, ‘outward conformity’ meant turning up at the parish church on a Sunday morning, listening to the Prayer Book service, and going home. It did not require enthusiasm. Many in the north of England, in country parishes far from London, kept old practices — saints’ days, holy wells, prayers for the dead — alongside attendance. The state was content with the appearance of compliance because punishing private belief was beyond its administrative reach. Key Fact Elizabeth aimed for outward conformity, not inner belief. The 1559 Settlement kept Catholic-style appearances (vestments, altars, ambiguous wording) but enforced Protestant doctrine through the Act of Supremacy and the 39 Articles. Both committed Catholics and hardline Puritans rejected the compromise; the rest were expected to attend church and keep their views private.

lessons.subject: history-aqa
lessons.title: The Northern Rebellion, excommunication and the missionary threat
lessons.text: A Decade of Catholic Threat The 1559 religious settlement had survived its first ten years, but in 1568 the situation changed sharply. Mary, Queen of Scots, fled into England after losing a Scottish civil war. As a Catholic with a strong claim to the English throne, she became an instant focus for any Catholic discontented with Elizabeth. Within twelve months, the country saw its largest rebellion of the reign; within fifteen months, the Pope declared Elizabeth no longer queen; within a decade, hundreds of trained Catholic missionaries were entering England in secret. This lesson follows that chain of events. The Northern Rebellion, November 1569 The Northern Rebellion was led by two great northern earls: Thomas Percy, Earl of Northumberland, and Charles Neville, Earl of Westmorland. Their grievances were both religious and political. They were Catholics who resented the 1559 settlement; they had lost influence in the north as Elizabeth promoted southern Protestants; and they were drawn into a wider plan to marry Mary, Queen of Scots, to the Duke of Norfolk and force Elizabeth to recognise Mary as her heir. Norfolk was arrested before he could act. On 14 November 1569 the earls and around 4,600 followers seized Durham Cathedral, tore up the English Prayer Book, and celebrated a Catholic mass for the first time in a decade. They marched south. But their numbers stalled below 6,000, the southern Catholics they hoped would rise stayed quiet, and a royal army under the Earl of Sussex moved north. By December the rebels had retreated; by January 1570 the earls had fled to Scotland; the rebellion was over. Around 450 rebels were hanged in their home villages on Elizabeth’s orders — a deliberately public punishment to deter further risings. Key Fact The Northern Rebellion of November 1569 was led by the Catholic earls of Northumberland and Westmorland. They seized Durham Cathedral, restored the Latin mass, and marched south — but failed to spread the rising. Around 450 rebels were hanged in their villages. The Papal Excommunication, 1570 In February 1570, Pope Pius V issued the bull Regnans in Excelsis . He declared Elizabeth a heretic, excommunicated her, and released English Catholics from their oath of allegiance to the Crown. In effect, the Pope told Catholics they no longer had a religious duty to obey their queen — and that those who deposed or killed her would be acting in line with Catholic conscience. The bull was a turning point. Before 1570, the regime could treat its Catholic subjects as politically loyal even if religiously different. After 1570 every recusant was, on paper, a potential traitor. The political consequence was almost immediate: a 1571 Treasons Act made it treason to import the bull or to call the queen a heretic, and recusancy fines began their long climb. The longer-term consequence was psychological: from 1570 the regime treated militant Catholicism as a national-security problem, not a pastoral one. How news of the bull reached England In May 1570, a London Catholic named John Felton nailed a copy of the papal bull to the gates of the Bishop of London’s palace. He was arrested, tortured, and executed in August. His action made the bull famous overnight. Felton’s defiance set the pattern for what missionary priests would later do: take a public stand for Catholic conscience and accept the consequences. He was canonised by Pope Paul VI in 1970. The Missionary Priests From the 1570s, English Catholics responded to the bull with a quiet counter-offensive. William Allen, an English Catholic in exile, opened a seminary at Douai (in modern Belgium) in 1568. Its purpose was to train English-speaking Catholic priests and send them home to keep Catholic worship alive. The first Douai priests reached England in 1574. Around 471 trained priests would enter England by the end of the reign. From 1580 the Jesuit Order joined the mission — the most famous arrivals being Edmund Campion and Robert Persons in June 1580. The missionaries were not, in their own minds, plotters. Their task was sacramental: to hear confessions, say mass and baptise. But the regime saw them differently. After Regnans in Excelsis, any priest entering England in secret was assumed to be working for the queen’s deposition. The 1585 Act of Parliament made it treason for any Catholic priest trained abroad to be in England at all. Around 130 priests were executed during the reign, including Campion in 1581. Persons escaped to the Continent and went on writing in support of Catholic claims to the English throne. The link to later plots and the Armada The chain from 1569 to 1588 is unbroken. The Northern Rebellion fed Mary’s reputation as a Catholic figurehead. The 1570 bull made her a focus for plots, including Ridolfi (1571), Throckmorton (1583) and Babington (1586). Each plot tightened the laws against Catholics; tighter laws drove some English Catholics to Spain; Spanish willingness to invade was hardened by Mary’s execution in 1587. The Armada of 1588 is the last act of the same drama. Examiners reward answers that show this interaction, rather than treating each event in isolation. The Threat in Context It is easy to overstate the danger. The Northern Rebellion fizzled out within seven weeks; no English Catholic gentry of consequence joined the missionaries; ordinary Catholic parishioners mostly continued to attend church and pay their fines. But the regime felt the threat acutely. Walsingham’s intelligence service was built largely to track priests and plotters; the Privy Council’s correspondence in the 1580s is dominated by Catholic anxieties; and the increasingly harsh recusancy laws are unintelligible without 1569 and 1570 in the background. Key Fact The 1570 papal bull Regnans in Excelsis released English Catholics from loyalty to Elizabeth and was the moment the regime began to treat Catholicism as a national-security problem. The 1571 Treasons Act, the missionary priests, and the 1585 Act against them all flow directly from this turning point.
