lessons.subject: history-aqa
lessons.title: Mary, Queen of Scots: plots, trial and execution
lessons.text: Mary’s Arrival in England, 1568 In May 1568, Mary, Queen of Scots, crossed the Solway Firth in a small fishing boat and threw herself on Elizabeth’s mercy. She was Elizabeth’s first cousin once removed, a Catholic, the great-granddaughter of Henry VII, and — for any English Catholic who rejected Henry VIII’s divorce — the rightful queen of England. She was also a fugitive: deposed by Scottish lords, suspected of involvement in the murder of her second husband, Lord Darnley, and forced to abdicate in favour of her infant son James. Elizabeth would not see her in person. Instead, Mary was placed under guard, first at Carlisle, then at a series of country houses in central England. She would remain a prisoner for the next nineteen years. Key Fact Mary, Queen of Scots, fled to England in May 1568 after losing a Scottish civil war. She was Elizabeth’s Catholic cousin and a rival claimant to the English throne. She was held under house arrest for 19 years, until her execution in February 1587. Why Mary Was a Problem — Not Just a Prisoner Killing Mary in 1568 was politically impossible. She was an anointed queen, a guest of the Crown, and a foreign sovereign. Releasing her was equally dangerous: she would head for France or Spain and become a Catholic figurehead abroad. So Elizabeth chose a third option — house arrest — and hoped the problem would solve itself. It did not. Mary was a magnet for every Catholic who hoped to undo the 1559 settlement. Within eighteen months her presence had helped trigger the Northern Rebellion of 1569, which aimed to free her and marry her to the Duke of Norfolk. A common confusion at GCSE is between Mary, Queen of Scots, and Mary I — Elizabeth’s Tudor half-sister, who died in 1558 and never appears in this depth study. Mary Queen of Scots is the Stuart cousin, captured 1568, executed 1587. Keep them apart. A Decade of Plots Three major Catholic plots between 1571 and 1583 turned on Mary’s claim to the throne. The 1571 Ridolfi Plot proposed a Spanish invasion timed with an English Catholic rising; Norfolk was executed for treason in 1572, although Elizabeth spared Mary. The 1583 Throckmorton Plot proposed a French invasion led by Mary’s cousin the Duke of Guise; Walsingham’s agents discovered it and the Spanish ambassador was expelled. Each plot tightened the laws against Catholics and pushed Parliament to demand Mary’s execution. Each time, Elizabeth refused. Why Elizabeth held back Elizabeth’s reluctance to execute Mary was not only personal. Killing an anointed queen would set a dangerous precedent for her own throne. It risked open war with Catholic France and Spain. It would damage her image as a merciful ruler. And it would martyr Mary — arguably making her more dangerous dead than alive. For nearly twenty years, Elizabeth chose the political risk of keeping Mary alive over the legal risk of killing her. The Babington Plot, 1586 The third and decisive plot was led by Anthony Babington, a young Catholic gentleman, in the summer of 1586. The plan was to assassinate Elizabeth, free Mary, and place her on the throne with Spanish backing. The plotters wrote to Mary in cipher, smuggling letters in and out of her household at Chartley Hall hidden inside a beer barrel. What Babington did not know was that the brewer was working for Walsingham. Every letter was intercepted, copied, and read before being sent on. Walsingham’s code-breaker Thomas Phelippes deciphered them, including Mary’s reply approving the plot. The trap closed in August 1586. Babington and his fellow conspirators were arrested, tried, and executed by hanging, drawing, and quartering in September. Mary was put on trial in October at Fotheringhay Castle . The court of nobles and judges found her guilty of complicity in plotting Elizabeth’s death. Key Fact The 1586 Babington Plot was uncovered when Walsingham’s agents intercepted ciphered letters smuggled in beer barrels at Chartley Hall. Mary’s written approval of Elizabeth’s assassination became the legal evidence that justified her trial and execution. Execution at Fotheringhay, 8 February 1587 Parliament demanded Mary’s death; Elizabeth signed the death warrant in February 1587 but afterwards claimed she had not meant it to be carried out. Her secretary William Davison was sent to the Tower as a scapegoat. On 8 February 1587 Mary was beheaded in the great hall of Fotheringhay Castle. She wore a red petticoat — the colour of Catholic martyrdom — and forgave the executioner. The first axe blow missed her neck and struck her skull; it took three blows to kill her. The execution shocked Catholic Europe. Philip II of Spain, who had until then preferred a Mary-led coup to a full invasion, now committed himself to launching the Armada the following year. Mary’s son James VI of Scotland, who would become James I of England in 1603, made a formal protest but accepted a pension and stayed quiet. Within England, the immediate effect was relief: the long source of Catholic plotting was gone. Significance over time Mary’s execution is the hinge between the religious crisis of the 1570s and the war crisis of 1588. Without her death, Philip II might have continued to wait. Without her death, the recusancy laws of the late 1580s would not have had Parliament’s full support. And without her death, the 1603 succession of her son James to the English throne — the Stuart line that would rule until 1714 — would have been politically impossible. Examiners reward students who follow these consequences across years rather than treating 1587 as an isolated event.

lessons.title: Conflict with Spain and the Spanish Armada (1588)
lessons.text: From Cold War to Open War By 1588 England and Spain had been drifting towards war for two decades. Three pressures converged. First, religion: Spain was the leading Catholic power in Europe, England was Protestant, and the Pope had excommunicated Elizabeth in 1570. Second, the Netherlands: when Dutch Protestants rebelled against Spanish rule in 1568, Elizabeth gave them quiet financial help, then in 1585 sent the Earl of Leicester with 6,000 English troops — an open act of war. Third, the sea: English ‘Sea Dogs’ like Drake and Hawkins had been raiding Spanish treasure ships in the Caribbean since the 1560s, and Drake’s circumnavigation (1577–1580) returned with around £400,000 in Spanish silver. The execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, in February 1587 was the final trigger; Philip II of Spain decided invasion was now the only answer. Key Fact The Spanish Armada of 1588 had three long-running causes — religion, the Dutch Revolt, and English raiding of Spanish treasure ships — and one trigger: the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, in February 1587. Philip’s Plan Philip’s plan was an enterprise of England. The Armada — around 130 ships carrying 19,000 soldiers and 8,000 sailors — would sail from Lisbon up the English Channel, link with the Duke of Parma’s veteran army of 30,000 in the Spanish Netherlands, and ferry them across to land in Kent. London would fall, Elizabeth would be deposed, and a Catholic government installed. The plan depended on something Philip never quite secured: a deep-water port in the Netherlands where Parma’s flat-bottomed barges could meet the Armada in safety. Without that, the rendezvous would have to take place at sea — a far harder operation. Drake delayed the launch by a year. In April 1587 he led a raid on Cadiz harbour, burning around 30 Spanish ships and destroying barrel staves needed to hold the Armada’s salt pork and water. Spanish supply, already strained, was set back by twelve months. Drake called it ‘singeing the King of Spain’s beard’. English Naval Reform By 1588 the English navy had been quietly transformed. Sir John Hawkins, as Treasurer of the Navy from 1577, had redesigned the fleet around race-built galleons : longer, narrower, lower in the water, faster, and carrying long-range bronze cannon along the side. Spanish ships, by contrast, were built for boarding: high-sided, packed with soldiers and short-range guns, designed to come alongside an enemy and fight hand to hand. English crews trained to use this advantage at distance. Their tactic was to stand off, fire broadsides at long range, then turn away before the Spanish could close. The Spanish fleet, commanded by the inexperienced Duke of Medina Sidonia after the death of his predecessor, sailed in a tight crescent formation designed to keep the English boarders out — but unable to chase a faster enemy. The English commanders Lord Howard of Effingham was Lord High Admiral and overall commander — a Catholic from a noble family, chosen partly to reassure waverers. Sir Francis Drake was vice-admiral and the public face of the campaign. Sir John Hawkins commanded one of the four squadrons. Sir Martin Frobisher commanded another. None of them had fought a battle on this scale before, but together they represented the most experienced fighting sailors in Europe. The Battle in the Channel, July 1588 The Armada was sighted off the Lizard on 19 July 1588. According to legend, Drake refused to leave his game of bowls at Plymouth Hoe, saying there was time to finish it and beat the Spaniards too. The story is probably fiction; the tide was wrong for sailing immediately. Over nine days the two fleets fought running battles up the Channel — off Eddystone, Portland Bill, and the Isle of Wight. Neither side scored a decisive blow. Spanish ships proved hard to sink with cannon fire alone; English supplies of powder and shot ran low. On 27 July Medina Sidonia anchored at Calais, expecting Parma’s army to be ready. It was not — Parma had no deep-water port and his barges were still inland. The Armada was caught in an exposed roadstead with no rendezvous and no clear next move. Fireships and Gravelines, 28–29 July In the early hours of 28 July, the English sent eight fireships — old hulks packed with pitch and gunpowder, set alight and aimed at the Spanish anchorage. The Spanish cut their cables in panic to escape, breaking the crescent formation. The next morning, off the Flemish coast at Gravelines, the English fleet caught the scattered Spaniards in close action and pounded them at short range for nine hours. Several Spanish ships were sunk or captured; many more were damaged. The fleet was driven north into the North Sea. Key Fact The Armada was beaten by a combination of factors: English race-built ships and long-range cannon (technology), stand-off broadside tactics, the fireship attack at Calais and the failure of the Parma rendezvous (command), and the storms that wrecked many ships off Scotland and Ireland on the long voyage home (weather). The Long Way Home Unable to return down the Channel, Medina Sidonia took the surviving Armada north around Scotland and west of Ireland. Atlantic storms wrecked dozens of ships on the Irish coast; thousands of Spanish sailors and soldiers drowned or were killed by English forces ashore. Of the original 130 ships, only around 67 returned to Spain. Some 20,000 men were lost — most to disease and shipwreck, not battle. Elizabeth’s famous speech at Tilbury — ‘I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too’ — was given on 9 August 1588 to the army assembled to repel an invasion that was already failing. The ‘Protestant Wind’ misconception A common GCSE misconception is that the weather alone defeated the Armada — the so-called ‘Protestant Wind’. Weather mattered greatly on the voyage home, but the Armada had already lost its strategic purpose at Calais on 28 July, before the worst storms began. The fireships, the failure of the Parma rendezvous, and English ship design were what broke the formation. The storms then finished the job. Examiners reward students who weigh all four factors rather than collapsing the answer into ‘the weather’.

lessons.subject: history-aqa
lessons.title: Living standards, fashion and the rise of the gentry
lessons.text: A ‘Golden Age’ for Whom? The phrase Golden Age was not invented by Elizabethans. It was attached to the late Tudor period by later writers who admired its theatre, exploration and architecture. For some people in the 1570s and 1580s the label fits well. The middling sort — landowners, merchants, lawyers, prosperous farmers — saw a real rise in living standards. They built bigger houses, bought more clothes, ate more meat, and read more books. Yet for the labouring poor the same decades brought rising prices, harvest failures, and harsher Poor Laws. The same period that produced Shakespeare also produced the 1572 statute classifying jobless beggars as criminals. A useful working answer is “Golden Age for some, harder times for others” — not the soft ‘everyone benefited’ story. Key Fact The ‘Golden Age’ label was applied to Elizabethan England by later writers and reflects only part of the picture — the lives of the gentry and middling sort. The same decades brought a sharp rise in vagrancy, harsher recusancy laws, and harvest failures for the poor. The Rise of the Gentry The biggest social change of the period was the rise of the gentry . They sat below the great nobility but above ordinary farmers and town tradesmen. Three things expanded their wealth and power. First, the dissolution of the monasteries under Henry VIII (1536–40) had thrown vast amounts of church land onto the market; gentry families bought it cheap and farmed it for profit. Second, rising food prices in the 1570s and 1580s meant that those who owned land made more money — the same harvest, sold at higher prices. Third, Elizabeth deliberately drew the gentry into local government: most justices of the peace, sheriffs, militia captains, and members of Parliament were gentry. By 1600 they ran county England. Their growing confidence shows in their houses. The Elizabethan style favoured tall windows of small leaded panes, decorative chimneys, and ground-plans shaped like the letter E or H — a play on Elizabeth’s own name. Hardwick Hall in Derbyshire, built for Bess of Hardwick from 1590, was famous for having “more glass than wall”. Glass was expensive; using it on this scale was a public statement of wealth and loyalty to the queen. The ‘Great Rebuilding’ Historians sometimes call the period 1570–1640 the Great Rebuilding because so many gentry, yeomen and prosperous craftsmen replaced timber and wattle houses with brick or stone, added a second floor, and put glass in the windows. Houses gained separate bedrooms, fireplaces in private rooms, and proper chimneys instead of central hearths. Better housing reflected real gains in middling-sort wealth — but the labouring poor lived in cottages little changed from the medieval period. Living Standards: What Improved For those above the labouring poor, daily life became more comfortable across Elizabeth’s reign. Diet improved: meat, dairy and white wheat bread replaced the rye and pottage of poorer households. Pewter replaced wood for tableware in middle-class homes; chairs replaced benches; mattresses stuffed with feathers replaced straw. Demand for new goods grew — books, clocks, mirrors, sugar, tobacco, and increasingly tea and spices brought in by long-distance merchants. The rise of the print trade in London put cheap pamphlets, almanacs and Bibles within reach of literate households for the first time. Fashion and the Sumptuary Laws Elizabethan fashion was loud and political. Wealthy men wore doublets, padded breeches, and starched white ruffs that grew comically large by the 1580s. Wealthy women wore farthingales (hooped skirts), tight bodices, and elaborate sleeves. Colour mattered: rich purple, deep red, black with silver, pearls and embroidery were status symbols. Elizabeth’s own image was a careful performance — the white face paint, jewelled gowns, and the unmarried ‘Virgin Queen’ persona were political tools, not personal vanity. The regime tried to control all this through sumptuary laws — rules about which colours and fabrics each social rank could wear. A 1574 statute, for example, restricted purple silk and cloth-of-gold to the royal family and the highest nobility. The laws are revealing because they barely worked: the very fact that gentry and merchants kept dressing above their rank shows how blurred the social hierarchy was becoming. Key Fact Sumptuary laws (such as the 1574 statute) restricted which colours and fabrics each social rank could wear. Their repeated reissue and weak enforcement show that gentry and merchants were increasingly dressing above their rank — evidence the social hierarchy was loosening, not tightening. Limits of the Boom It is important not to mistake the gentry’s gains for general prosperity. The rising food prices that enriched landowners squeezed labourers; harvest failures in 1586, 1594 and 1596–97 caused real hunger; wages did not keep pace with prices for the unskilled. The growth of London (around 50,000 in 1500, perhaps 200,000 by 1600) brought wealth and culture but also overcrowded slums, plague, and the new visible poverty that scared the regime into the Poor Laws of 1572, 1576 and 1598. The Golden Age and the Poor Law era are the same period. Why this matters for the exam The 16-mark essay often invites students to weigh “how far” Elizabethan England was a Golden Age. Top-band answers do not just list achievements (theatre, exploration, the Armada). They balance the gentry’s rise and middling-sort prosperity against the poverty, harvest failures, and persecution that ran in parallel. The fact that the same decade gave us the rise of the gentry and the 1572 Vagabonds Act is the heart of a strong answer.

lessons.subject: history-aqa
lessons.title: Poverty, vagrancy and the Elizabethan Poor Laws
lessons.text: A Sharp Rise in Visible Poverty Poverty was not new in 1568, but its scale and visibility changed dramatically across Elizabeth’s reign. Contemporaries reported large bands of jobless men and women on the roads, swelling crowds of beggars in market towns, and overcrowded slums in London. Modern historians estimate that perhaps half of England’s population lived close to the poverty line by 1600, with around a quarter falling below it in years of crisis. The Elizabethan poor were not a single group: they ranged from elderly widows unable to work, to skilled craftsmen squeezed by inflation, to the so-called sturdy beggars — able-bodied wanderers feared as criminals. Key Fact Elizabethan poverty had four main drivers: a population rise from around 3 million in 1551 to around 4 million by 1601, sharp inflation in food prices, the enclosure of common land for sheep farming, and bad harvests — especially the crisis years of 1586, 1594 and 1596–97. Causes of the Increase Population growth was the deepest cause. England’s population grew by roughly a third between 1551 and 1601 — from around 3 million to around 4 million — outpacing food production. More mouths chasing the same harvests pushed prices up. Wages did not keep pace: a craftsman’s real wage in 1600 was substantially lower than in 1500. Enclosure made things worse for many. Landowners fenced off common fields for sheep, evicting tenants and removing the grazing and gleaning rights that had cushioned poor families. Sheep farming needed fewer workers than arable farming, so jobs disappeared. Bad harvests were the trigger. The 1586 harvest failed; 1594, 1595 and 1596 produced what contemporaries called “the four wet years”; 1596–97 saw genuine famine in parts of the north and Cumbria. The cloth trade, which employed thousands in East Anglia and the West Country, suffered repeated slumps. The dissolution of the monasteries decades earlier had also removed the largest single source of charity for the rural poor — abbeys had run almshouses and food doles that no longer existed by Elizabeth’s reign. Why returning soldiers added to the problem From the 1580s the war with Spain in the Netherlands and Ireland sent thousands of English soldiers and sailors back to England with no land, no wages, and often serious wounds. Veterans of the Armada campaign were paid late or not at all and many turned to begging. They are part of the reason the 1593 statute distinguished ‘maimed soldiers’ as a deserving category, separate from sturdy beggars. Attitudes to the Poor Elizabethans drew a hard line between two kinds of poor: the impotent poor — the elderly, disabled, orphaned, sick, who could not work — and the able-bodied poor, expected to work or be punished. The impotent poor were treated with sympathy and given parish relief. The able-bodied jobless were treated with suspicion: many people genuinely believed sturdy beggars were lazy criminals, that begging spread plague, and that wandering bands threatened public order. Religious thinking made this worse: Calvinist Protestants tended to see worldly success as a sign of God’s favour and poverty as a sign of moral failure. The fear of disorder mattered more than charity in driving government action. The Privy Council’s correspondence in the 1580s and 1590s is full of warnings of riots in market towns when grain prices spiked. The Oxfordshire Rising of 1596 — a small attempted uprising by a few dozen poor men — was a real warning of what hunger might unleash. The Poor Laws of 1572, 1576 and 1598 Parliament responded with three major statutes. The 1572 Vagabonds Act, the harshest, classified jobless beggars as criminals: a first offence brought whipping and ear boring; a second made them felons; a third meant the death penalty. But the same act introduced the first compulsory poor rate — a property tax raised parish by parish to support the deserving poor. The 1576 Poor Relief Act required every town to provide raw materials (wool, flax, hemp) so that the able-bodied could be put to work, and to set up a House of Correction for those who refused. The 1598 Act for the Relief of the Poor, consolidated into the famous 1601 Poor Law, made the parish the basic unit of welfare for over two centuries afterwards. Each parish elected unpaid Overseers of the Poor to collect the poor rate and distribute relief. Key Fact The Elizabethan Poor Laws of 1572, 1576 and 1598 split the poor into deserving (impotent) and undeserving (sturdy beggars), funded relief through a compulsory parish poor rate, set the able-bodied to work, and made the parish — not central government — the unit of welfare for the next 250 years. How the System Worked in Practice The 1598 system rested on the parish. Each year, parishioners elected two Overseers of the Poor from the better-off householders. The overseers collected the poor rate, paid pensions to the elderly and disabled, found apprenticeships for poor children, and bought materials for the workhouse. Vagrants caught wandering were whipped and sent back to their parish of birth or last legal settlement — the principle that one’s home parish was responsible for one’s welfare. The London authorities went further with their own institutions: Bridewell handled idle vagrants, Bethlem the mentally ill, and Christ’s Hospital orphaned children. How effective were the Poor Laws? Strengths: the Poor Laws were the first nationally organised system of welfare in Europe; they channelled local charitable energy through the parish; they survived virtually unchanged until 1834. Weaknesses: relief depended on the willingness of parishes to tax themselves — some did, others did not. The harsh treatment of vagrants did little to address root causes. And the deserving/undeserving distinction obscured the fact that most able-bodied poor were jobless because there was no work, not because they refused to take it. Examiners reward students who weigh both sides.

lessons.subject: history-aqa
lessons.title: English sailors: Hawkins, Drake, Raleigh and exploration
lessons.text: Why Elizabethans Took to the Sea By the 1560s, Spain and Portugal already controlled most known sea routes to the Americas, Africa and Asia, and treated those routes as their private property. England was a small, second-rank naval power that wanted in. Three things drove Elizabethan sailors to push past Spanish and Portuguese monopolies: the lure of profit from gold, silver and spices; the religious rivalry that made attacking Catholic Spain seem patriotic; and Elizabeth’s willingness to license private captains to do what her navy could not officially do. The most famous of these captains were John Hawkins, Francis Drake and Walter Raleigh — all West Country gentlemen, all closely connected to the court. Key Fact Hawkins ran the first English slaving voyages in the 1560s and later redesigned the navy. Drake circumnavigated the globe between 1577 and 1580 and was knighted by Elizabeth on board his ship. Raleigh launched the failed Roanoke colony in 1585–87, England’s first attempt at settling North America. John Hawkins and the First Slaving Voyages John Hawkins made three slave-trading voyages between 1562 and 1568. He sailed to West Africa, where he seized or bought captive Africans, then crossed the Atlantic to sell them to Spanish colonists in the Caribbean in exchange for sugar, hides and pearls. Hawkins’s voyages broke the Spanish trade monopoly and made him — and his investors, including Elizabeth herself — a large profit. The third voyage ended in disaster at San Juan de Ulua in 1568 when a Spanish fleet ambushed Hawkins’s ships, killing most of his men. The young Francis Drake was on the voyage and barely escaped. He never forgave Spain. Hawkins’s most lasting contribution was not the slaving but what he did afterwards. From 1577, as Treasurer of the Navy, he redesigned English warships into the lighter, faster, more heavily gunned vessels known as ‘race-built’ galleons. These were the ships that would defeat the Armada eleven years later. The slaving voyages themselves are a moral stain on the period: Hawkins’s coat of arms, granted by Elizabeth, openly featured a bound African captive. How big was Elizabethan English slaving? Hawkins’s three voyages trafficked an estimated 1,200–1,400 Africans across the Atlantic. This was tiny compared with the later British slave trade of the 1700s, which trafficked millions, but it set a legal and commercial precedent: an English crew, with royal investment, treating human beings as cargo. After Hawkins, English slaving paused for about a century — until renewed and industrialised after 1660 — but the Elizabethan voyages are the start of that history, and modern historians and museums increasingly stress this part of the ‘Golden Age’ story. Francis Drake’s Circumnavigation, 1577–1580 In December 1577 Drake left Plymouth with five ships on a secret royal commission to raid Spanish ports along the Pacific coast of South America. By the time he returned to Plymouth in September 1580 he had sailed all the way around the world — only the second commander in history to do so, after the Portuguese-Spanish expedition of Magellan-Elcano in 1522. Drake had passed through the storms of the Strait of Magellan , raided the unprotected Spanish ports of Valparaiso and Callao, captured the treasure ship Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion (nicknamed the Cacafuego ), claimed the coast of California for Elizabeth as ‘New Albion’, and sailed home across the Pacific and Indian Oceans. The financial return was extraordinary. Drake brought back gold, silver and jewels worth perhaps £400,000 — more than a year of normal Crown income. Investors received roughly £47 for every £1 they had risked, and Elizabeth’s personal share allowed her to clear most of her foreign debts. In April 1581 she came on board Drake’s ship the Golden Hind at Deptford and knighted him on deck. Spain was furious: Philip II called Drake ‘ El Draque ’ (‘the Dragon’) and demanded his execution. Elizabeth refused. Key Fact Drake’s circumnavigation lasted from December 1577 to September 1580. It made England the second nation to sail around the globe, brought back roughly £400,000 in plunder, struck a propaganda blow against Spain, and provided a model for later English voyages of trade and exploration. Walter Raleigh and the Roanoke Colony Walter Raleigh was a court favourite of Elizabeth in the 1580s — soldier, poet, courtier, and from 1585 the holder of a royal patent to plant an English colony in North America. He never sailed to Roanoke himself but bankrolled and organised the expeditions. The first attempt, in 1585, landed about 100 men on Roanoke Island off the coast of modern North Carolina. Short of food and clashing with the local Algonquian inhabitants, the colonists abandoned the site after a year and sailed home with Drake when he stopped by on his way back from raiding the Caribbean. A second colony was planted in 1587 under Governor John White and included around 115 men, women and children — among them White’s daughter Eleanor Dare, who gave birth to Virginia Dare , the first English child born in the Americas. White returned to England for supplies, but the war with Spain meant no relief ship reached Roanoke until 1590. By then the colony had vanished. The only clue was the word ‘CROATOAN’ carved on a post. The fate of the Roanoke colonists has never been confirmed. Why Roanoke failed Roanoke failed for several connected reasons. The site was poorly chosen: shallow inlets made it hard to resupply by sea. The colonists arrived too late in the season to plant crops and quickly became dependent on the Algonquian for food, which broke down into violence. Raleigh’s organisation underfunded the venture, and the war with Spain pulled every available ship into home defence after 1588. England would not successfully plant a North American colony until Jamestown in 1607 — a generation later. Raleigh himself fell from royal favour in 1592, was imprisoned by James I in 1603, and was eventually executed in 1618. The Bigger Picture: Voyages, Trade and Profit Behind the famous names, Elizabethan sea power had a wider dimension. The Muscovy Company (1555) traded with Russia. The Levant Company (1581) opened trade with the Ottoman Empire. The East India Company, founded just before the end of the reign in 1600, would eventually overshadow them all. Privateering — legalised piracy under royal licence — brought thousands of Spanish prizes home to West Country ports. The Sea Dogs, as Drake’s circle were known, were both heroes of national propaganda and pirates by Spanish definition. By 1603 England was not yet an imperial power, but the institutional and commercial base for empire was visibly being assembled.

triage.why_not: This lesson is primarily narrative and chronological—it tells the stories of three sailors, their voyages, their profits, and their outcomes. The content works through exposition: *why* they sailed (profit, religion, royal licence), *what* they did (specific routes, treasures, battles), and *what happened* (success, failure, impact). The lesson builds understanding through concrete historical detail and causal explanation, not through manipulation or discovery. An interactive would only decorate these stories rather than teach the causal or conceptual relationships better. Even a 'choose-a-path' (what if you were Raleigh?) or 'step-through-a-process' (Drake's route) would be peripheral—the real learning is in the prose: why England needed to break Spanish monopolies, how Hawkins's naval redesign mattered more than his slaving, why Roanoke failed on multiple fronts. A student needs to *read and understand* these connections, not manipulate variables.

lessons.title: The Elizabethan theatre and attitudes towards it
lessons.text: A New Kind of Entertainment Before Elizabeth’s reign, plays in England had mostly been performed by travelling troupes in inn yards, in the halls of great houses, or as religious pageants run by town guilds. By 1600 something very different was happening: purpose-built playhouses outside the city walls of London were drawing audiences of two or three thousand people, several afternoons a week, paying a penny each. The Elizabethan public theatre was new in scale, in business model and in cultural reach. It was also a flashpoint — loved at court, distrusted by the City of London authorities, and attacked outright by Puritan critics. Key Fact Elizabethan theatre boomed because of three connected factors: noble patronage that protected actors from vagrancy laws, the rise of a paying urban audience with disposable income, and Elizabeth’s personal taste for plays at court. The first purpose-built public playhouse, The Theatre, opened in 1576 in Shoreditch. Patronage and the Companies Acting was not legally a respectable profession. The 1572 Vagabonds Act listed unattached actors alongside sturdy beggars and threatened them with whipping unless they had a noble patron. The result was that every successful Elizabethan acting company was named after a great lord. The Lord Chamberlain’s Men — led by Richard Burbage, with William Shakespeare as a sharer — were patronised by the Lord Chamberlain at court. The Admiral’s Men, who performed at the Rose, were patronised by the Lord Admiral. Patronage gave companies legal cover, social respectability and access to court performances. The companies themselves were small. A typical company had around twelve sharers (men who owned a stake in the business), a few hired men for smaller parts, and four or five boy apprentices who played all the female roles — women were not allowed on the public stage. Plays were performed in repertory: a different play each afternoon, six days a week, with new plays added constantly. Playwrights such as Shakespeare, Christopher Marlowe and Ben Jonson wrote at speed for these companies. How a public playhouse worked Playhouses were polygonal wooden buildings, open to the sky in the middle, around three storeys high. Audiences stood in the central yard for one penny — these were the groundlings — or paid two pennies for a seat in the covered galleries, with cushions an extra penny on top. Performances ran in the afternoon because there was no artificial lighting. Special effects were limited but inventive: cannon fire, trapdoors, suspended thrones lowered from the ‘heavens’ above the stage, and pig’s blood for stabbings. An Audience of Everyone The most striking thing about an Elizabethan playhouse audience was its mix. Apprentices, dock workers and prostitutes rubbed shoulders with merchants, country gentry visiting London, courtiers and foreign visitors. The Spanish ambassador watched alongside soldiers and sailors. A penny was within reach of even a working Londoner: one Tudor commentator complained that apprentices were skipping work to stand at plays. This breadth of audience is one reason Shakespeare’s plays move between high poetry, sword fights, jokes about bodily functions and royal politics within a single scene — he was writing for a paying public that contained every social rank. The cultural ambition of the plays grew quickly. Christopher Marlowe’s Doctor Faustus (c.1592) and Tamburlaine (1587) brought blank verse and big philosophical themes to a popular audience. Shakespeare’s histories — Henry V (1599), the Henry VI trilogy, Richard III — turned recent English politics into a public conversation. By 1600, Elizabethan playwrights were producing work that historians of literature treat as the foundation of modern English drama. Opposition: City of London and the Puritans Not everyone approved. The City of London Corporation — the merchant council that ran the City inside its medieval walls — banned public playhouses from operating on its territory from 1574. The Corporation gave four reasons: playhouses spread plague by drawing crowds; they attracted pickpockets, prostitutes and brawlers; they pulled apprentices away from honest work; and they encouraged immorality. This is why almost every Elizabethan playhouse stood just outside the City’s jurisdiction — in Shoreditch to the north (The Theatre, the Curtain), or south of the river in Southwark (the Rose, the Swan), where the Corporation’s writ did not run. Puritan critics went further. Puritans argued that the theatre was sinful in itself — it taught vanity, glorified violence, mixed the sexes (boys playing women), and tempted people from honest work and worship. The Puritan minister Philip Stubbes’s Anatomy of Abuses (1583) attacked plays as ‘the schools of vice’ and called for them to be shut. London preachers blamed plague outbreaks on God’s anger at the playhouses. During serious plague, the Privy Council itself ordered playhouses closed — in 1592–94, in 1603 and several times after — partly to control infection, partly to placate the City and the Puritans. When the Puritans came to power in the 1640s they would close the theatres entirely, for eighteen years. Key Fact Opposition to the theatre came from two main directions. The City of London Corporation banned playhouses from 1574 because they spread plague, drew pickpockets and pulled apprentices from work. Puritans went further and called the theatre sinful in itself. This is why playhouses were built in Shoreditch and Southwark, outside the City’s jurisdiction. Theatre and the Court Against this opposition the theatre had a powerful protector: Elizabeth herself. The Queen’s Men was an acting company set up in 1583 specifically to perform for her at court, and the Lord Chamberlain’s Men performed at Whitehall and Greenwich during the winter season. Court patronage gave the theatre a status the Puritan press could not undo while the Queen lived. The Master of the Revels and royal licensing A 1581 royal proclamation set up the Master of the Revels to license plays before performance — a system that protected the companies as much as it censored them, since a licensed play could not be banned by the City of London Corporation. The boom of the 1590s — the decade of Romeo and Juliet and Henry V , when several new playhouses were built south of the Thames — happened with the Queen’s active blessing.

lessons.title: The Spanish Armada: Historic Environment 2027
lessons.text: A Site Made of Water Your specified site for 2027 is not a building. The Spanish Armada campaign of 1588 is examined as a historic environment: the Channel and its winds, the ports on each shore, an exposed anchorage at Calais, the sandbanks off the Dutch coast, and the storm-lashed route home around Scotland and Ireland. The 16-mark question will ask how far a study of the Armada supports some statement, and the marks sit exactly where this lesson looks: in how geography shaped the outcome. Lesson 8 covers why Philip launched the Armada; this lesson follows the fleet through the environment that destroyed it. The Plan and Its Geographical Flaw Philip’s plan — the Enterprise of England — was not for the Armada to invade on its own. Its 130 ships carried perhaps eighteen thousand soldiers, but the real invasion army was the Duke of Parma’s veteran force in the Spanish Netherlands. The Armada’s job was to sweep up the Channel, join Parma, and escort his troops across the narrow sea in barges. The flaw was on the map from the start: Spain held no deep-water port anywhere along the invasion coast. Parma’s embarkation ports at Dunkirk and Nieuwpoort were shallow, fringed by sandbanks, and watched by Dutch flyboats that could sail where galleons could not. The Armada therefore had nowhere safe to wait, and the rendezvous depended on a fleet and an army, hundreds of miles apart with no fast communication, arriving in the same place at the same moment. Key Fact There was no deep-water port in friendly hands between Spain and Parma’s army. The Armada could reach the Netherlands coast — but it could not wait there safely, and Parma’s shallow ports were blockaded by Dutch flyboats his escorts could not clear. Two Fleets Built for Different Battles The commander Philip appointed after his best admiral died, the Duke of Medina Sidonia, led a fleet built around big, high-sided ships packed with soldiers, designed to grapple and board — to turn a sea fight into a land fight on wet decks. The English fleet, under Lord Howard of Effingham with Francis Drake as his deputy, was built on the opposite theory: race-built galleons , faster and more weatherly, carrying long-range culverins , crewed by sailors rather than soldiers. Just as important was where each fleet slept: the English operated from their own ports — Plymouth, then the anchorages up-Channel — with powder, shot, food and repairs a day away. Every mile the Armada sailed took it further from any harbour that could help it. Up the Channel: The Crescent and the Weather Gauge The Armada was sighted off the Lizard on 19 July 1588, and warning beacons carried the news along the coast faster than any rider. For a week the two fleets ran east up the Channel, and the fighting settled into a pattern set by wind and formation. Medina Sidonia sailed in a disciplined crescent, his strongest warships at the tips, transports sheltered inside — a formation the English could harass but not break. The English, holding the weather gauge , attacked from windward at Plymouth, Portland Bill and the Isle of Wight, staying at culverin range and refusing to close where Spanish soldiers could board. A week of running battle cost the Armada only a few ships — but it reached Calais with ammunition low, no port to enter, and Parma not ready. The beacon network: England’s early-warning system Chains of hilltop beacons ran along the south coast and inland to London — pitch-soaked fires on high ground, each visible from the next. Lit in sequence, they could carry the alarm across southern England in hours. The system is a site feature worth naming: it meant the English fleet and the militia mustering at Tilbury reacted to the Armada’s movements at a speed Philip’s planners, working on months-old information, could not match. Calais: An Anchorage That Doomed the Fleet On 27 July the Armada anchored off Calais — not a harbour, just an open roadstead, exposed to wind and enemy alike, because there was nowhere else to go. Parma sent word he needed almost a week more, and his barges could not move while the flyboats prowled the banks. The English needed no week. On the night of 28 July they sent eight fireships, stuffed with pitch and gunpowder with guns left loaded to fire as they burned, down the wind into the anchorage. Against ships at anchor in the dark, packed close, the threat was terror itself. The Spanish captains cut their anchor cables to escape — and the crescent, which gunfire had never broken, ceased to exist in a single night. The cut cables would collect their price later: a fleet without anchors cannot hold itself off a storm coast. Key Fact Escaping the fireships, the Spanish captains cut their cables and abandoned their best anchors on the seabed off Calais. Weeks later, on the storm coasts of Scotland and Ireland, ships that could not anchor were driven ashore — a one-night decision at the site with a months-long consequence. Gravelines and the Wind That Changed Twice Off Gravelines on 29 July the English finally fought the battle they wanted: close enough for their guns to hurt, far enough to refuse boarding, against a scattered enemy short of shot. Several Spanish ships were sunk or driven ashore and many more were battered. Then the environment nearly finished the campaign at a stroke: the wind pushed the fleet towards the Zeeland sandbanks, shoaling water with no sea room, and only a shift of wind at the last moment let the Armada claw off into the North Sea. The same shift settled the campaign’s direction — with the English behind them and the wind foul for the Channel, the only way home was north-about, around Scotland and Ireland. The Long Way Home The route home killed more ships than the English had. Autumn gales caught a battered fleet on some of the most dangerous coasts in Europe; ships without anchors, with storm-damaged hulls and starving crews, were wrecked in numbers on the Scottish isles and above all on the west coast of Ireland. Perhaps half the fleet never reached Spain, and thousands of men died of drowning, disease and starvation — far more than died to English gunfire. Victory did not spare the victors either: typhus and dysentery swept the English fleet in the weeks after Gravelines, and sailors who had saved the kingdom died unpaid in the ports they had defended. Elizabeth’s famous appearance before the army at Tilbury came while the Armada was already limping north — the image of victory, minted as the environment completed it. Using the Campaign as Your Site Work in chains of feature and consequence. The missing deep-water port explains why the Armada was at anchor in an open roadstead at Calais; the roadstead explains why fireships worked; the cut cables explain the wrecks on the Irish coast; the sandbanks off Zeeland explain why Gravelines nearly ended everything; the home ports and beacon chains explain English speed and stamina; the north-about route explains why a fleet that lost few ships in battle lost half its strength getting home. Whatever the statement in the question, tie each claim to a named feature of this seaborne site and its consequence.

lessons.title: Kenilworth Castle: Historic Environment 2028
lessons.text: A Castle Rebuilt Around One Guest Kenilworth Castle is your specified site for the 2028 exam. It is a medieval fortress in Warwickshire — Norman keep, great mere, John of Gaunt’s hall — but the exam is not really about the Middle Ages. It is about what Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, did to the place in the 1570s, and above all about nineteen days in July 1575 when he staged the most lavish entertainment of the reign for Elizabeth I. Read the site properly and it opens up half your course: the court, royal progresses , the marriage question, and the politics of spending money to be loved. Dudley and the Gift of a Castle Kenilworth came to Dudley from the queen herself: she granted him the castle in 1563, the year before she made him Earl of Leicester. He was her favourite — the man she called her ‘eyes’, master of the horse, privy councillor, and for decades the most plausible husband she never took (Lesson 3). The gift was typical of how Elizabeth ruled her court: favour made visible in land and stone. What Dudley then spent on the place turned a royal gift into a royal argument — a castle rebuilt as a machine for entertaining one woman. Key Fact Elizabeth granted Kenilworth to Robert Dudley in 1563. For her visits he added a four-storey tower of state apartments — Leicester’s Building — raised a grand new gatehouse, modernised the medieval keep with great windows, and laid out a privy garden fit for a queen. Reading the Site: What Leicester Built The additions are still legible in the ruins, and each one is evidence. Leicester’s Building was a slender four-storey block of glittering state apartments, built so the queen and her ladies could lodge in modern comfort beside the medieval great hall — a private palace bolted onto a fortress. The gatehouse gave arriving courtiers a fashionable first impression (and survives intact, because later owners made it a house). The Norman keep was kept — twelfth-century mass declaring the antiquity of the place — but Leicester punched huge windows into it, dressing ancient strength in Elizabethan glass. And below the walls he laid out the privy garden : terraces, obelisks, an aviary of exotic birds, a marble fountain — recorded in such detail by an eyewitness that English Heritage rebuilt it in 2009. Around it all lay the mere , the vast lake that had made medieval Kenilworth almost siege-proof and that Leicester turned into a stage. Notice what he did not build: nothing military. Like Acton Burnell three centuries earlier, Kenilworth in the 1570s shows defences repurposed as display — but here the purpose was sharper than status. Every stone was aimed at the queen’s opinion. The Nineteen Days of 1575 Elizabeth had visited before — 1566, 1568, 1572 — but the visit of 9 to 27 July 1575 outdid everything in the reign: the longest stay she made at any courtier’s house. Leicester met her with a floating ‘Lady of the Lake’ welcoming her to a castle of legend; fireworks were reportedly heard twenty miles away; there was hunting by day and masques by night, bear-baiting, an Italian tumbler, and a swimming pageant in the mere where a performer as Arion, the legendary musician of Greek myth, rode a mechanical dolphin. Contemporaries claimed the entertainment cost Leicester a fortune — a figure of a thousand pounds a day was bandied about, and even if gossip inflated it, the true cost would have crushed most noble families. We know the detail because two eyewitness accounts survive: a long gossipy letter attributed to Robert Langham, a minor court official, and the poet George Gascoigne’s Princely Pleasures . What was Leicester actually asking for? Most historians read 1575 as Leicester’s last grand bid for Elizabeth’s hand. The pageants said it almost openly — masques of marriage and of a lady released from an enchanted lake — and one planned entertainment pressing the theme was, tellingly, never performed; historians suspect the queen declined to hear it. She was forty-one, and hopes of the Leicester match were fading; and she left Kenilworth unmarried, as she left everywhere. For your exam, the visit is the marriage question (Lesson 3) staged in fireworks — and refused. What the Site Shows About Elizabethan England Kenilworth in 1575 is the court system working at full power. It shows how progresses let Elizabeth be seen by her people and fed at her courtiers’ expense — power displayed while someone else paid. It shows what favour was worth: a castle, offices and income flowed to Dudley, and he poured them back into loyalty spectacular enough for the whole kingdom to hear about. It shows the marriage question as living politics, played out in allegory before thousands. And it shows the propaganda machinery of the reign — poets, pageants and print carrying the event far beyond Warwickshire. The gossip, expense and spectacle of those nineteen days are as much a primary source for Elizabeth’s rule as any statute. Key Fact Two eyewitness accounts preserve the 1575 visit: the letter attributed to Robert Langham describing the festivities and the garden, and George Gascoigne’s Princely Pleasures at Kenilworth . Detail from the Langham letter guided English Heritage’s 2009 reconstruction of the Elizabethan garden. The Site Afterwards and in the Exam Leicester died in 1588, deep in debt. The castle passed on, was slighted after the Civil War in 1650 — the keep’s north side blown out, the mere drained — and settled into ruin. Today English Heritage keeps the shell, the gatehouse, the rebuilt garden and the empty basin of the mere. In the 16-mark question, chain features to meanings: Leicester’s Building → the cost of hosting the queen; the garden and pageants → courtship politics; the mere as stage → medieval strength repurposed as theatre; the gift of 1563 → how favour worked. Then weigh the site against your contextual knowledge of the court, progresses and the marriage question.

triage.idea: By labelling features of Kenilworth's layout (Leicester's Building, the mere, the privy garden, the gatehouse, the keep), students see how every physical element was deliberately designed to serve a single political purpose: impressing the queen.

spec.title: Label Kenilworth, Then Explain Why
spec.teaches: Every feature Leicester added to Kenilworth was chosen to serve one political purpose: winning Elizabeth's favour and hand.
spec.interaction: The student sees an illustrated cross-section of Elizabethan Kenilworth with five glowing pins on unlabelled features. They pick a feature-name chip (Leicester's Building, the gatehouse, the keep, the privy garden, the mere) and drop it on the pin they think it names; a wrong drop bounces back and adds a mistake. Once all five are correctly named, a second bank of 'political purpose' chips appears (e.g. 'cost of hosting the queen', 'medieval strength turned into theatre') and the student must drag each purpose onto the feature it explains, again with wrong drops bouncing back. The task is only finished when every feature is both named and chained to its correct historical purpose — getting the label right but the reasoning wrong still counts as incomplete.
